flashcards.detail: Revisit it when a model is deprecated or rate limits change; both invalidate common assumptions.

flashcards.back: A table assigning each activity or decision to who is Responsible for doing it, who is Accountable for the outcome, who must be Consulted and who is only Informed. It prevents gaps such as legal reviewing too late.
flashcards.detail: Name security, legal, compliance and operations during discovery; finding a veto holder late is expensive.

flashcards.back: A schedule of who receives which information, how often and in what form, such as executive summaries, demos, metric reports and incident notices, matched to each audience's concerns.
flashcards.detail: Executives want value and risk, security wants controls and data flow, operations want runbooks and service objectives: same facts, different views.

flashcards.back: The full cost of running a solution over its life: model usage, retrieval and infrastructure, integration and engineering, evaluation, human review time, monitoring and support, training and change management, not just the token bill.
flashcards.detail: Token spend is often a minority of the total in high-oversight workflows.

flashcards.back: The ratio of measured benefits to total cost, built from baseline numbers, pilot results (automation rate, error and rework changes) and a complete cost model, shown with ranges and stated assumptions rather than a single optimistic figure.
flashcards.detail: A defensible business case uses cost per completed task and a sensitivity analysis.

flashcards.back: A short, dated document capturing one significant design decision: the context, options considered, criteria, the choice made, its consequences and when to revisit it, kept alongside the design so the reasoning survives staff changes.
flashcards.detail: Handy for 'why this model tier?' questions months later, when a newer model ships.

flashcards.back: A table that scores candidate options against weighted criteria such as accuracy, latency, cost, security and effort, making trade-offs explicit and discussable instead of argued from preference.
flashcards.detail: Agree the weights with stakeholders before scoring, and check whether the winner changes when the weights move.

flashcards.back: A small, time-boxed build that tests whether the core idea is feasible and valuable on real data, aimed at answering a few risky questions rather than at production quality.
flashcards.detail: Do not ship it as is: it typically lacks evaluation depth, security review, monitoring and support.

flashcards.back: A limited live trial with real users and real workflows, often with extra human oversight, used to measure outcomes against acceptance criteria and gather feedback before wider rollout.
flashcards.detail: Choose representative users; a friendly team makes results look better than they will be at scale.

flashcards.back: A formal checkpoint between lifecycle phases, such as discovery to design or pilot to production, where agreed criteria (evaluation results, security review, operational readiness, budget) must be met before work proceeds.
flashcards.detail: Gates make go or no-go a measurement, not a mood.

flashcards.back: A contractual commitment to a customer on measurable service levels, such as availability and response time, with defined consequences if missed. It should promise only what the architecture and its dependencies can sustain.
flashcards.detail: Do not promise more than your least reliable dependency without fallbacks and graceful degradation.

flashcards.back: An internal target for a measured service level, for example 99 percent of answers within 5 seconds, usually set tighter than the external commitment, tracked through indicators and used to decide when reliability work takes priority.
flashcards.detail: For LLM systems add quality objectives (accuracy on sampled traffic) beside latency and availability.

flashcards.back: The amount of unreliability a service may incur within an objective over a period, for example 1 percent of requests. The remaining amount guides whether to ship risky changes or pause for stability work.
flashcards.detail: Gives product and engineering one shared number instead of an argument.

flashcards.back: A paid service tier that gave requests priority over standard traffic, with fewer overload errors, under committed capacity. New capacity commitments are no longer sold, although existing ones run to the end of their contract.
flashcards.detail: Do not build an availability promise on buying it; design for retries, fallbacks and headroom. The standard tier is best-effort.

flashcards.back: Designing a system to keep serving a reduced but acceptable experience when a dependency fails or is slow, for example showing search results without a generated summary, serving a cached answer, queuing for later or handing off to a person.
flashcards.detail: Plan it per dependency, test it, and tell users clearly when they are in degraded mode.

flashcards.back: Estimating peak demand in requests and tokens and comparing it with rate limits, quotas and budgets well before launch, then requesting higher limits, smoothing load, caching and ramping traffic gradually.
flashcards.detail: Tier increases take time, and sudden traffic jumps can trip acceleration limits.

flashcards.back: The people side of a rollout: engaging affected users early, training them, setting honest expectations about what the AI can and cannot do, naming champions, providing a feedback channel and phasing adoption.
flashcards.detail: Technical success with unprepared users still fails. Claude Code's champion and communications kits are examples.

flashcards.back: A concise record for a deployed AI system covering its intended use, out-of-scope uses, data and model versions, evaluation results by slice, known limitations, human-oversight design and owners, kept current for reviewers and operators.
flashcards.detail: Answers stakeholders who ask 'what can this do and where does it fail?' and supports audits.

flashcards.back: A picture of how data moves through the solution, from sources through prompts, tools, model providers and storage to outputs, marking trust boundaries, sensitive data and retention points.
flashcards.detail: Security and privacy reviewers ask for it first.

flashcards.back: Step-by-step operating instructions for a specific situation, such as a burst of 429 errors, a model retirement, a suspected injection or a harmful output, naming who acts, which dashboards to check, how to roll back and whom to notify.
flashcards.detail: Part of handoff; test it with a drill before launch.

flashcards.back: A pre-launch checklist review confirming that monitoring and alerts, runbooks, on-call ownership, rollback, capacity, security sign-off, training and support processes are in place before the system goes live.
flashcards.detail: Often the last phase gate before go-live.

flashcards.back: A short period right after launch with intensified monitoring, rapid fixes and close contact with users and stakeholders, before the solution moves to normal support.
flashcards.detail: Staff it with the build team, then hand over steady-state ownership.

flashcards.back: Managing prompts, templates and model settings as versioned, reviewed, tested artifacts with change history, a release tag recorded on every request and the ability to roll back, instead of editing live text in place.
flashcards.detail: Without it, a quality drop cannot be traced to a change.

flashcards.back: The stages Anthropic uses for each model: active (fully supported), legacy (no more updates, may be deprecated), deprecated (still works but not recommended, with a replacement and retirement date) and retired (requests fail). Publicly released models get at least 60 days' notice before retirement.
flashcards.detail: Partner platforms (Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud) set their own schedules. Audit use with the Console usage export by key and model.

flashcards.back: A planned move from one model version to another: inventory usage, read the migration notes for rejected parameters, recount tokens, audit prompts, run the evaluation suite side by side, shadow or canary, then cut over with rollback ready, well before the retirement date.
flashcards.detail: Newer models can reject parameters older code sets and read old prompt wording more literally.

flashcards.back: A runtime switch that turns a code path, prompt version or model on for chosen users or percentages without redeploying, enabling gradual rollout, quick rollback and separation of deployment from release.
flashcards.detail: Use it for canary exposure of a new model and as a kill switch for risky behavior.

flashcards.back: The umbrella name for organization policy in Claude Code that takes precedence over user and project configuration and can lock permissions, MCP servers, plugins, hooks and network destinations, whichever delivery route carries it.
flashcards.detail: Highest tier of the settings hierarchy. Array settings such as permission rules merge, so developers can add entries but not remove managed ones.

flashcards.back: Claude Code policy configured in the claude.ai admin console (Teams and Enterprise) and fetched from Anthropic's servers at startup and refreshed hourly, needing no device management. It is a client-side control rather than a security boundary on unmanaged devices.
flashcards.detail: Setting forceRemoteSettingsRefresh makes clients exit instead of starting without fresh policy.

flashcards.back: Claude Code policy deployed to devices through MDM profiles, registry policies or a settings file in a protected system directory. Operating-system permissions keep users from editing it, so it gives stronger guarantees than delivery from the cloud.
flashcards.detail: Among managed sources the order is server-managed, then plist or machine registry policy, then the file, with the user-writable registry lowest.

flashcards.back: Claude Code rules evaluated in the order deny, then ask, then allow, where the first match decides the outcome. A narrow allow cannot carve an exception out of a broad deny, and the rules are enforced by the tool rather than by the model.
flashcards.detail: Use them with sandboxing: rules match command text, while the sandbox enforces access at the OS level.

flashcards.back: Managed-only settings that stop developers from loosening policy, such as making managed settings the sole source of permission rules and disabling the mode that skips permission prompts.
flashcards.detail: Keys: allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly and permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode. Similar locks exist for hooks and MCP servers.

flashcards.back: Administrator control over which MCP servers Claude Code may use: allowlists and denylists, an option that honors only the managed allowlist, or a deployed managed file that provides a fixed set of servers to every user.
flashcards.detail: Stops developers from connecting unvetted servers; pair it with plugin marketplace restrictions.

flashcards.back: Managed settings that restrict which plugin marketplaces developers may add or install from, block sideloading flags and command-based plugin sources, and let administrators distribute vetted plugins, skills and hooks.
flashcards.detail: Keys include strictKnownMarketplaces and strictPluginOnlyCustomization. Treat plugins like software installs.

flashcards.back: A managed-policy instruction file placed at a protected system path on each machine, loaded into every Claude Code session and impossible for users to exclude, used for company standards, security policy and compliance rules.
flashcards.detail: It is guidance only: it shapes behavior but does not enforce. Use permission rules, hooks or sandboxing for rules that must hold.

flashcards.back: A markdown file Claude Code reads at the start of every session to learn project commands, conventions and gotchas it cannot infer from the code. Keep it short (under about 200 lines), check it into git, and move situational instructions into skills or path-scoped rules.
flashcards.detail: A bloated file makes Claude ignore parts of it. Running /init generates a starter.

flashcards.back: User-defined commands that Claude Code runs automatically at lifecycle points, such as before or after a tool call or when a turn ends. Because they run deterministically, they enforce rules (format after edit, block a command, require tests to pass) instead of hoping the model complies.
flashcards.detail: In a PreToolUse hook, exit code 2 blocks the action. CLAUDE.md is guidance; hooks are guarantees.

flashcards.back: A dashboard showing adoption and impact: active users and sessions, suggestion accept rate, lines accepted and, on Teams and Enterprise with GitHub connected, merged pull requests that contain Claude-assisted code. Console API customers get usage and spend views.
flashcards.detail: Contribution metrics are deliberately conservative, unavailable for ZDR organizations, and do not cover usage through cloud providers.

flashcards.back: Opt-in export of Claude Code metrics (sessions, tokens, cost, lines changed, tool decisions) and events to your own collector, switched on by an environment variable and best pinned in managed settings. Prompt text is redacted unless explicitly enabled.
flashcards.detail: The only way to stream per-user cost into your own stack in near real time; it works with every provider, including cloud-platform deployments.

flashcards.back: A proxy that sits between Claude Code (or other clients) and the model provider to centralize credentials, per-user usage tracking, spend limits and request logging, and to route by data sensitivity.
flashcards.detail: Anthropic offers a self-hosted Claude apps gateway. Sessions that go through any gateway are not eligible for the HIPAA configuration.

flashcards.back: An adoption approach in which engineers who already use the tool well share reusable prompts and wins in channels the team already reads, answer questions publicly, run a weekly show-and-tell and pair on first tasks, so adoption is carried by habits rather than announcements.
flashcards.detail: Claude Code's champion kit assumes a modest weekly time budget and offers a thirty-day playbook.

flashcards.back: Ready-to-adapt launch material for a developer-tool rollout: an organization-wide announcement, an executive-sponsor variant, tips messages and FAQ answers, plus a pre-send checklist (channel created, install tested, data-handling link ready, a named owner, one concrete first task).
flashcards.detail: Rewrite it in your own voice and swap in real tasks from your codebase.

flashcards.back: Running Claude Code from scripts, CI jobs and hooks with a prompt flag and no interactive session, with options for allowed tools, turn limits, permission mode and structured output formats, so it can lint, review or triage automatically.
flashcards.detail: Store credentials as pipeline secrets, cap work with a turn limit, and keep the permission set minimal.

flashcards.back: A check Claude can run itself and read the result of, such as a test suite, build, linter or screenshot comparison, given in the prompt or enforced by a hook, so work is verified by evidence instead of by the developer eyeballing it.
flashcards.detail: The difference between a session you watch and one you can leave running.

flashcards.back: Claude Code's automatic snapshots of files before edits, with each prompt creating a restore point, letting a developer roll back conversation, code or both with a double escape or a slash command. Changes made through shell commands are not captured.
flashcards.detail: Not a replacement for git; it lets developers try risky approaches cheaply.

flashcards.back: A Claude Code permission mode in which the agent researches the codebase and proposes changes for approval without editing files, used for complex or risky work and for building trust with new users.
flashcards.detail: Cheaper than re-work after a wrong direction.

flashcards.back: A Claude Code permission mode in which a separate classifier model reviews most actions, blocking risky ones such as scope escalation or hostile-content-driven steps while letting routine work proceed without prompts; organizations can turn it off.
flashcards.detail: Reduces prompt fatigue; explicit deny rules still apply.

questions.question: A freight forwarder wants to cut the time staff spend answering shipping-exception emails. Replies need the customer's shipment record and the carrier's policy documents, and a staff member must approve each reply before it is sent. Which solution shape best fits?
options: One augmented call per email with a lookup tool and cached policy text, producing a draft for staff approval
A planner, researcher, writer and reviewer team of agents that negotiate each reply among themselves before staff see it
An autonomous agent that sends replies straight to customers and updates the shipment system once its accuracy looks high
A keyword rules engine that picks one of fifty canned replies per email, which avoids model cost and any need for review
questions.explanation: The input is varied free text, the needed data is one lookup plus stable policy text, and a person approves the output, so one well-augmented call is the simplest shape that meets the need. A four-agent team adds token overhead and hand-off loss with no context-pollution, parallelism or specialization reason. A fully autonomous agent removes the approval the business requires and adds risk. A canned-reply rules engine cannot handle the variety of real exceptions.
questions.whyTested: Translate a business problem into the simplest Claude-based shape that satisfies its constraints.

questions.question: A support platform receives billing questions, technical faults and account-closure requests. Each type needs different instructions, tools and escalation rules, and a lightweight classifier can sort incoming messages accurately. Which pattern should the architect choose?
options: Evaluator-optimizer: draft a reply, have a critic review it, and loop until the draft passes, for every message type
Routing: classify each message first, then dispatch it to a specialized prompt and tool set for its category
Voting: run all three handlers on every message and take the majority answer, so no single handler can be wrong
Orchestrator-workers: let a central model invent subtasks for each message at run time, then merge the replies
questions.explanation: Distinct categories that can be classified accurately are the textbook case for routing: each handler is tuned for one kind of request, so optimizing for one does not hurt another. Evaluator-optimizer polishes a single output and does not separate categories. Voting triples cost and produces conflicting answers from handlers built for different jobs. Orchestrator-workers is for subtasks that cannot be predicted in advance, which is not the situation here.

questions.question: A migration tool must replace a deprecated library across customer repositories. How many files change, and what each change involves, depends on the repository and cannot be known before the tool inspects it. Which pattern fits best?
options: Prompt chaining with a fixed list of steps that is applied to every repository in the same order, with a gate after each
Routing by file extension, with one specialized prompt per programming language handling all of that language's files
Sectioning into three pre-defined parallel calls, each given an equal share of the repository's files to rewrite
Orchestrator-workers: a central call inspects the repository, decides the subtasks, and delegates them to worker calls
questions.explanation: When the subtasks depend on the input and cannot be listed in advance, a central model should decompose the task at run time and delegate, which is orchestrator-workers. A fixed chain or a pre-defined split assumes you already know the structure of the work, and routing by extension only chooses a prompt without deciding how many changes to make.
questions.whyTested: Orchestrator-workers differs from sectioning in that the split is decided at run time.

questions.question: A localization team translates marketing copy in which tone and idiom matter. First drafts often miss nuance, but reviewers can state clear criteria (register, brand terms, idiom) and a second model can apply them. Which pattern improves output quality most directly?
options: Parallel voting: translate the copy three times and publish whichever wording appears most often across the drafts
Routing: send each target language to a different model and publish that model's first draft after a spell check
Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts, another critiques against the criteria, and the loop repeats until it passes
Prompt chaining: draft once, then have a second call reformat the draft to the house style and publish it
questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer fits when criteria are explicit and iterative feedback measurably improves the result, which is exactly translation nuance with a rubric. Voting gives diverse attempts to compare but never refines a draft, routing only picks a model, and a reformatting chain adds no critique.
questions.whyTested: Know the signs of a good evaluator-optimizer fit: clear criteria and feedback that improves results.

questions.question: A prototype uses five agents (planner, implementer, tester, reviewer, documenter) to deliver features. Logs show each hand-off losing context, and the team is spending more tokens coordinating than building. What is the best redesign?
options: Add a sixth coordinator agent whose only job is to manage the hand-offs and summarize each stage for the next agent
Let one agent own a feature together with its tests, and keep a separate agent only for black-box verification
Switch every agent to the strongest model tier, so that fewer details are lost whenever work changes hands
Make all five agents read and write one shared transcript so that nothing is ever lost between the roles
questions.explanation: Splitting by type of activity (planner, tester, reviewer) is problem-centric decomposition and creates a telephone game in which each recipient lacks the reasoning behind earlier steps. Splitting along context boundaries keeps the building agent's context intact, and a verifier that only runs tests needs little of it. A coordinator adds another hop, a bigger model does not restore lost context, and a shared transcript recreates the bloat the split was meant to avoid.

questions.question: A research assistant must compare twelve vendors against a rubric using public sources. Each vendor can be researched independently, the work is high value, and the final report must synthesize all twelve. Which decomposition is most appropriate?
options: A role-based pipeline of searcher, summarizer, formatter and reviewer agents that all share one growing transcript
One agent that researches the twelve vendors one after another inside a single conversation, however long it grows
A lead agent that spawns one research subagent per vendor, each in its own context, and synthesizes their findings
One subagent per paragraph of the final report, each writing its paragraph from the full pile of raw research notes
questions.explanation: Independent research paths are a recommended decomposition boundary: each subagent works in a clean context, can run in parallel, and returns a condensed result so the lead's context stays focused. A role-based pipeline is problem-centric and loses context at each hand-off, a single sequential conversation suffers context pollution as the sources pile up, and splitting by report paragraph cuts across the shared evidence.

questions.question: A lead agent delegates 'fix the failing checkout test' to a subagent, which then spends many turns rediscovering which repository, file and error to look at. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?
options: The subagent's output limit is too low; raise its max_tokens so that it can keep exploring the codebase for longer
The subagent's model is too small for the task; upgrade it to the same model that the lead agent uses
A subagent inherits none of the parent's conversation; put paths, error output and constraints in the delegation prompt
The subagent needs the lead's full system prompt copied into its own so that it behaves exactly like the lead
questions.explanation: A subagent starts with a fresh context, and the only thing passed from parent to child is the task prompt, so anything it needs (paths, errors, decisions, constraints) must be written into that prompt. A larger token limit or model does not supply missing facts, and copying the lead's system prompt gives it the lead's role but still none of the task context.

questions.question: A claims-intake system extracts fields from submitted forms and writes them to the core claims system. Adjusters often correct the extracted values, but the team keeps no record of those corrections and accuracy has not improved in months. Which architectural element is missing?
options: A caching layer in front of the extraction call, so that repeated forms are not processed twice by the model
A second extraction pass at higher effort for every form, with the two results compared before they are written
A larger context window, so that more of the earlier form history fits into each extraction request
A feedback loop that captures adjuster corrections, links them to inputs and prompts, and feeds evaluations
questions.explanation: The pipeline stops at output, so nothing learns from human corrections. A complete design closes the loop: corrections become labeled examples for evaluation sets and prompt or retrieval changes. Caching, extra passes and a bigger window may change cost or latency but give the team no new information about where the system is wrong.

questions.question: A team will run a nightly agent that processes large document sets for up to two hours using shell and file tools. They want to avoid building a sandbox, an event store and a tool-execution layer, and their data terms allow Anthropic to hold session history. Which option best fits?
options: The Message Batches API, because the job runs overnight and batch requests cost half as much as standard ones
Claude Managed Agents, with a cloud environment, one session per run and a session budget as a cost ceiling
The Messages API with their own loop, sandbox and persistence, for maximum control over every step of the run
The Agent SDK in containers the team operates, with transcripts persisted to their own database
questions.explanation: Managed Agents supplies the hosted harness, sandbox, persisted events and long-running sessions, which is what the team wants to avoid building. The Batches API processes independent Messages requests at a discount, not a stateful loop with shell tools. The other two options mean the team operates the loop, sandbox or processes itself, the opposite of the stated goal.
questions.whyTested: Match the hosting option to who should operate the loop and sandbox.

questions.question: An internal developer portal must embed a coding agent with file editing, shell access, permission rules and hooks inside a service the company operates. The team does not want to write the tool loop. Which option fits?
options: The Claude Agent SDK, embedded in the company's own service so the loop runs in a process the team operates
Claude Managed Agents, because Anthropic should host the agent loop and run the sandbox for the portal
The Messages API with a hand-written agent loop and the team's own tool execution and permission layer
The MCP connector alone, which gives the model tools without any agent loop of its own
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK packages Claude Code's loop, built-in tools, permissions and hooks as a library that runs in a process you operate, which matches both the embedding requirement and the wish to avoid writing the loop. Managed Agents moves execution to Anthropic-hosted infrastructure rather than the company's service. The raw Messages API leaves the loop to the team, and a connector supplies tools but no loop.

questions.question: A CFO asks how the proposed support assistant's architecture serves the cost and performance-SLA pillars. Which response is strongest?
options: It uses the largest model for every ticket, so quality risk is minimal and no routing, tuning or monitoring is needed
The chosen model has a low price per million tokens, which is the only cost metric that matters to the business
A multi-agent design is used, which demonstrates transformation and shows leadership how modern the system is
Small model for routine tickets, cached shared prefix, and dashboards for cost per resolved ticket and p95 latency
questions.explanation: A defensible answer ties specific design decisions to measurable outcomes: routing and caching reduce cost per resolved ticket, and latency is tracked against the service target. Using the largest model everywhere ignores cost, per-token price alone misses turns and retries, and choosing multi-agent for show adds cost without addressing either pillar.

questions.question: A support agent can search the knowledge base, draft replies, issue refunds and close accounts. Refunds above a threshold and account closures are hard to reverse. Where should human approval be placed?
options: Before every tool call, including knowledge-base searches, so that nothing happens without a person's approval
Before refunds above the threshold and before account closures, while searching and drafting run freely
Nowhere in the flow; the system prompt tells the agent to ask a person whenever it is unsure
After all actions complete, in a weekly review of the logs that flags anything that looks wrong
questions.explanation: Approval gates belong where the blast radius is large and reversal is hard. Gating every call defeats the automation, relying on the prompt alone leaves a high-impact action to probabilistic behavior, and a weekly log review detects problems after the damage is done.

questions.question: A 40-step data-reconciliation agent sometimes misreads a column mapping at step 3, and every later step then builds on the mistake. Restarting costs hours. Which change best contains the damage?
options: Raise max_tokens so the agent has more room to reason carefully about each step before it acts
Tell the agent in the prompt to double-check every step twice and to stop if anything looks inconsistent
Add verification checkpoints after milestones, and persist state so a run can resume from the last verified one
Run the same 40 steps in several parallel copies and keep whichever copy finishes first with a result
questions.explanation: Errors compound in long autonomous runs, so the design needs explicit verification points and durable state to resume from. More tokens and a request to be careful do not create a check that can fail, and racing duplicate runs spends more and can finish first with the same wrong assumption.

questions.question: A regulated insurer's intake process always follows the same six steps (identify policy, extract facts, check coverage rules, compute a summary, flag exceptions, produce a record). Auditors require a deterministic order with each step logged. Which design fits best?
options: An autonomous agent that plans its own steps for each claim and decides when the intake is complete
A single prompt that performs all six steps in one response and returns the finished record in one go
Orchestrator-workers, where a central model decides at run time which of the steps to run for each claim
A prompt chain with one focused call per step and programmatic gates between them
questions.explanation: A fixed, auditable sequence is what workflows are for: each step is a focused call, code enforces the order and gates can reject bad intermediate output, and every step is loggable. An autonomous agent or orchestrator makes the order the model's choice, and a single prompt hides the steps and offers no place to check them.

questions.question: A consumer chat feature must screen each user message for policy violations without adding noticeable delay to normal replies. Which design meets both needs?
options: Screen first, wait for the verdict, and only then start generating the answer to the user's message
Run the screening call and the answering call in parallel, and release the answer only if screening passes
Answer immediately and screen afterwards, retracting the reply if the screen fails once it has been shown
Ask a single call to screen the message and answer it in the same response to save a round trip
questions.explanation: Sectioning in parallel hides the screening latency behind the answering latency, while the gate keeps unscreened content from reaching the user. Sequential screening adds the full delay, answering first exposes the user to unscreened output, and combining both jobs in one call blurs two tasks that perform better when handled separately.

questions.question: A compliance team must analyze 3,000 policy documents, far more than fit in one context window, and each document can be analyzed independently. Cost matters. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Run one top-tier agent that reads the documents one after another in a single growing conversation
Paste as many documents as fit into one prompt and ignore the rest, since the answer is similar anyway
Lower the effort level of a single agent, since effort alone determines the size of the bill for this job
Partition the documents among lower-cost worker agents coordinated by an orchestrator that merges the results
questions.explanation: When the work is larger than one window, delegating partitions to lower-cost workers is the pattern that saved money in Anthropic's measurements, because the bill is the reading itself and lowering effort cannot shrink it. One growing conversation hits the window and context rot, and truncating the input silently drops most of the work.

questions.question: An executor on a lower tier stalls only on hard planning decisions, so the team adds a higher-tier model through the advisor tool. Early results show no quality gain, though the advisor definition adds prompt tokens to every request. What should the team check first?
options: Whether the executor really consults the advisor: measure the consult rate and compare with the executor alone at higher effort
Whether max_tokens is large enough for the advisor's reply to fit, since truncated advice would explain the missing gain
Whether to promote the advisor to be the executor on every turn, since the stronger model would always do better
Whether adding a second advisor from the same tier raises agreement and so gives the executor more confidence
questions.explanation: An advisor can help only when it is consulted. Measuring the consult rate, and comparing the pairing with the executor alone on its own effort curve, shows whether the tool adds anything for its cost. Promoting the advisor changes the architecture instead of diagnosing it, and the other two options do not address why no consultation benefit appears.

questions.question: Four teams propose multi-agent designs. Which proposal has the strongest justification for using more than one agent?
options: A three-phase feature build in which each phase depends on the previous phase's full reasoning and decisions
A five-tool FAQ assistant that answers short questions in a single turn, each with a one-line reply
A tightly coupled schema migration whose steps constantly depend on each other's intermediate state
Breadth-first competitive research across thirty independent sources, with findings condensed for a lead
questions.explanation: Multi-agent designs pay off for independent, parallelizable work whose bulky intermediate output should stay out of the lead's context. Sequential phases that share reasoning, tightly coupled steps and a small single-turn assistant all lose more to coordination than they gain.

questions.question: In Claude Managed Agents, a lead agent must ask a security specialist follow-up questions after the specialist's first report. Which mechanism fits?
options: A dynamic workflow run, because the threads of a run stay open so that the lead can ask follow-ups
Subagent delegation, because a subagent's thread persists and can receive follow-up messages
An advisor model, because it keeps working on the lead's behalf and can answer questions on demand
Separate sessions, because agents inside one session have no way to send messages to each other
questions.explanation: A subagent's thread stays available until archived, so the lead can send follow-ups and the subagent retains its earlier turns. The agent cannot message a workflow run's threads, which the server archives at the end of the run. An advisor is consulted for guidance mid-turn by the primary thread and does not hold a work stream, and sessions are not required for agents to coordinate.

questions.question: A scheduled Managed Agents job usually costs a few dollars but occasionally costs ten times that when it loops on a flaky tool. Finance wants a guaranteed ceiling per run. What should the architect configure?
options: A system prompt instruction telling the agent to stop and report when its costs seem unusually high
A lower max_tokens so each response is shorter and a looping run spends less on every turn
The Batch API discount, which halves the price of every request in the job and so halves the worst case
A session budget on every session or deployment, backed by a workspace spend limit as the final backstop
questions.explanation: A session budget is a platform-enforced ceiling: at the cap the session pauses rather than spending more. A prompt instruction is only guidance, a smaller output cap neither counts turns nor stops loops, and the Batch API is not available for Managed Agents sessions, which are interactive by design.
questions.whyTested: Programmatic enforcement beats prompt guidance where cost or consequences are severe.

questions.question: A contact-center assistant must deliver the first words of an answer within two seconds at the 95th percentile. About 80 percent of questions are simple FAQs; the rest need multi-step lookups. Which configuration best meets the SLA while controlling cost?
options: Use the highest tier at maximum effort for every question, so that quality never limits the experience
Route FAQs to the small tier at low effort, escalate complex cases, stream responses and cache the static prefix
Run a three-agent debate on every question and return the consensus answer as soon as two agents agree
Send every request through the Batch API for the discount and notify users when their answers are ready
questions.explanation: Routing matches model and effort to difficulty, streaming improves time to first token and caching shortens prefix processing, so the common case is fast and cheap while hard cases still get capability. The top tier at maximum effort misses the latency target, a debate multiplies latency and tokens, and batch results can take up to a day.

questions.question: Which requirement is the strongest signal that a fixed workflow should give way to a true agent loop?
options: The task always runs the same five steps in the same order, so the path can be written down in advance
The number and order of steps cannot be predicted and depend on what each tool call returns
Outputs must be reproducible step by step so that an auditor can replay exactly what happened
The request is a single classification with a fixed label set and a known list of examples
questions.explanation: Agents suit open-ended problems where the path cannot be hard-coded and the model must act on feedback from the environment. The other three describe predictable or auditable work, which a workflow or a single call serves better with less cost and risk.

questions.question: A prototype using one call with retrieval and three examples meets 92 percent of its quality target. The tech lead proposes a multi-agent redesign to close the gap. What is the best next step?
options: Approve the redesign, because adding more agents always raises accuracy by spreading work across them
Ship at 92 percent without examining the failures, since the prototype is already close to the target
Analyze the failing cases and try targeted fixes, such as retrieval, examples or effort, before adding agents
Move to the smallest tier to free budget for the redesign, then add agents to recover the lost quality
questions.explanation: The simplest-solution-first principle says to add complexity only when measurements show simpler options fall short. Failure analysis may reveal retrieval or example gaps that are cheaper to fix, and multi-agent systems often use several times the tokens without helping. Shipping blind skips the evidence, and downsizing the model works against the quality goal.

questions.question: A security team requires that the files and processes an agent touches stay on company infrastructure, yet it does not want to operate the agent loop itself. Session history may be stored by Anthropic. Which option fits?
options: Managed Agents with the default cloud sandbox, because Anthropic manages the container for each session
The Messages API with a loop hosted on company servers, with tools executed inside the company network
Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox on company infrastructure, so tools and files stay in-house
The Agent SDK in company-operated containers, with the company running every session's agent loop
questions.explanation: A self-hosted sandbox keeps tool execution and the filesystem on infrastructure the company controls while Anthropic still hosts the loop, though session history and tool inputs and outputs still go to Anthropic. The cloud sandbox moves files off site, and the other two satisfy residency but make the team operate the loop. If no conversation data may leave, the Agent SDK or Messages API on a platform the company controls would become the answer instead.

questions.question: A lead agent's answer quality drops after it delegates web research: each subagent returns its full 40,000-token browsing transcript. What design change is best?
options: Enlarge the lead's context window so that all the returned browsing transcripts can fit in it
Remove the subagents and have the lead run every search itself, which avoids any hand-off between agents
Ask the subagents to compress their transcripts into denser formatting before returning them to the lead
Have each subagent return a short structured finding with sources, keeping raw material in its own context
questions.explanation: The purpose of delegation is context isolation: helpers should explore widely and return a condensed result, often only one or two thousand tokens, so the lead's window holds signal. Returning raw transcripts defeats it. A bigger window does not stop context rot, and doing all searches in the lead's context creates exactly the pollution the subagents were meant to prevent.

questions.question: A three-hour research run fails after two hours because a tool times out, and the system restarts the entire run from the beginning. Which change gives the best resilience?
options: Retry the whole run automatically until it succeeds, with a pause between attempts to let the tool recover
Persist progress at checkpoints so a run resumes where it stopped, and report tool failures to the model
Shorten the prompt so the run finishes faster and is less likely to meet a tool timeout
Silently remove the failing tool and let the agent carry on with whatever other tools it has left
questions.explanation: Agents are stateful and long running, so restarts are expensive and the design should make resumption normal. Telling the model when a tool is failing lets it adapt, for example by trying another source. Blind full retries waste hours, a shorter prompt does not address failures, and silently dropping a tool hides a capability gap from both the model and the operators.

questions.question: One prompt asks the model to extract entities from a letter, classify the risk, and draft a response letter. Quality is uneven across the three tasks. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Add 'be careful and thorough' to the prompt so the model gives each of the three tasks equal attention
Move all the instructions to the end of the user message, where the model pays the most attention
Increase max_tokens so that the model has enough room to complete all three tasks in one response
Split the work into a chain of focused calls with a programmatic check between steps
questions.explanation: Decomposing a complex task into a chain makes each call easier and lets code verify intermediate results, trading a little latency for accuracy. Exhortations, instruction placement and a larger output cap do not change the fact that three different jobs compete inside one call.

questions.question: Which two observations suggest a single agent has outgrown its design and a multi-agent split may be justified? (Choose two.)
options: The work has three sequential phases that all depend on the same detailed reasoning from earlier steps
Independent subtasks, such as researching separate sources, could run at the same time
The agent handles short questions in a single turn using four well-described tools
Bulky intermediate results from one subtask are crowding out the context needed for later subtasks
The team would like each job title in the process (planner, tester, reviewer) to have its own prompt
questions.explanation: Context pollution and parallelizable independent work are two of the three situations in which several agents consistently beat one (the third is specialization of tools or instructions). A small single-turn assistant has nothing to split, sequential phases that share reasoning lose context at every hand-off, and sophistication is not a requirement.

questions.question: Which two are good reasons to use a dedicated verification subagent? (Choose two.)
options: It can judge the result fairly only after reading the builder's complete reasoning history
Verification needs little context from the builder, so the hand-off loses almost nothing
It roughly halves the token cost of the overall task by sharing the builder's context
It enforces an explicit checkpoint using tools such as a test runner or a schema validator
It removes the need to define success criteria, because the verifier decides what good looks like
questions.explanation: A verifier can black-box test an artifact against stated criteria, so it avoids the telephone-game losses of other splits and gives the workflow a hard checkpoint with the right tools. It does not need the builder's history, it adds a call rather than halving cost, and it works only if success criteria are defined.

questions.question: Which two actions in an order-handling agent most clearly warrant an approval gate? (Choose two.)
options: Looking up the shipping status of an order for a customer who asked
Refunding an order for an amount above a set monetary threshold
Drafting a reply that a person will review before it is sent
Deleting a customer account together with all of its stored data
Searching the help center for an article that answers the question
questions.explanation: Gates belong on actions that are costly or hard to reverse: large refunds and permanent deletions. Reads and drafts that a person reviews are low-impact and easily undone, so gating them only slows the flow.

questions.question: Which three conditions favor a predefined workflow over an autonomous agent? (Choose three.)
options: The problem is open-ended and the path cannot be hard-coded
The steps are known in advance and rarely change
Auditors need a deterministic, logged order of steps
The number of steps depends on what each tool call returns
Predictable latency and cost matter more than flexibility
questions.explanation: Workflows give predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks. When the number of steps depends on tool results or the path cannot be hard-coded, the model must direct the process, which is what an agent is for.

questions.question: A board paper must map the claims assistant's metrics to the business value pillars. Which two pairings are sound? (Choose two.)
options: Number of prompt templates written by the team, mapped to transformation
Average handle time per claim before and after launch, mapped to efficiency
Number of staff trained on the new tool, mapped to performance SLAs
p95 response time against the contractual target, mapped to performance SLAs
Parameter count of the selected model, mapped to cost control
questions.explanation: Handle time measures efficiency and latency against the contractual target measures performance. Counting templates or model parameters measures effort or size rather than business outcomes, and training numbers say nothing about meeting a response-time commitment.
questions.whyTested: Tie each architectural decision to a measurable outcome in the business value pillars.

questions.question: Which two statements about delegation in Claude Managed Agents are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Delegated agents can themselves delegate to further agents to any depth, with no limit on threads
Each delegated agent runs in its own session thread with its own conversation history
A delegated agent automatically starts with the lead agent's full conversation history in its context
Agents in a session share the same sandbox filesystem and vault credentials
The lead can send follow-up messages to the threads of a workflow run after it finishes
questions.explanation: Threads isolate each agent's context, but the agents share the sandbox and credentials, which is a reason to give delegated agents narrow toolsets. Delegated agents do not inherit the lead's conversation, workflow-run threads cannot receive follow-ups and are archived when the run ends, and delegation is limited to one level deep with a cap on child threads.

questions.question: Which two measures best contain compounding errors in a long autonomous run? (Choose two.)
options: A larger max_tokens on every call, so each step has room to explain its reasoning in more detail
Verification checkpoints after each milestone, so a bad assumption is caught before later steps build on it
Removing turn limits and stop conditions so that the loop has time to recover from its own mistakes
A final pass that repeats the whole chain from scratch and publishes whichever result arrives first
Durable, resumable state so that a failed run restarts from its last verified point instead of the start
questions.explanation: Checkpoints catch a bad assumption early and durable state avoids paying for the whole run again. Output limits do not detect errors, removing stop conditions invites runaway loops, and an unchecked repeat run can carry the same mistake.

questions.question: Anthropic's guidance for agentic systems is to start with the simplest solution that works and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
questions.explanation: Agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, so a single optimized call with retrieval and examples is often enough, and workflows or agents are added when measurements show the need.

questions.question: In a workflow the model decides which steps to run next, whereas in an agent the steps are fixed in code in advance.
questions.explanation: It is the other way around. In a workflow, code paths are predefined and the LLM fills steps in them; in an agent, the model directs its own process and tool use.

questions.question: Multi-agent systems typically use fewer total tokens than a single agent doing the same task.
questions.explanation: Duplicated context, coordination messages and result summaries make multi-agent systems use several times more tokens, 3 to 10 times in Anthropic's testing and about 15 times a chat in its research system. They are justified only when the extra thoroughness is worth that cost.

questions.question: A subagent automatically inherits the full conversation history of the agent that spawned it.
questions.explanation: A subagent starts with a fresh context. Apart from its own instructions, the only thing the parent passes is the task prompt, so needed facts must be written into it.

questions.question: Having the agent that implements a feature also write that feature's tests is an example of context-centric decomposition.
questions.explanation: The implementing agent already holds the context the tests need. Splitting at context boundaries, rather than by type of activity, avoids lossy hand-offs.

questions.question: A verification subagent usually needs the builder's full reasoning history to do its job.
questions.explanation: Verification can be done black-box: the verifier needs the artifact, the success criteria and tools to check them, which is why it avoids the telephone-game losses of other splits.

questions.question: A Claude Managed Agents session budget is enforced by the platform, whereas a system prompt asking the agent to save money is only guidance.
questions.explanation: At the budget the session pauses with stop reason budget_reached. A prompt instruction depends on the model's behavior and gives no guarantee, so use platform limits where cost or consequences matter.

questions.question: With the Messages API your code owns the tool-use loop, whereas Claude Managed Agents runs the loop on Anthropic's infrastructure.
questions.explanation: The Messages API gives direct model access and leaves the loop, tool execution and state to you (the SDK's tool runner can drive the loop in your process). Managed Agents is a hosted harness that runs them for you.

questions.question: Claude Managed Agents is currently eligible for zero data retention and for HIPAA business associate agreement coverage.
questions.explanation: Because sessions are stateful and store history, sandbox state and outputs server-side, Managed Agents is not currently eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA BAA coverage. You can delete sessions and uploaded files yourself.
questions.whyTested: Data-handling terms can decide the platform before features do.

questions.question: The evaluator-optimizer pattern works best when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative feedback measurably improves the output.
questions.explanation: The two signs of a good fit are that responses visibly improve with articulated feedback and that a model can supply that feedback. Without clear criteria the loop adds cost and no quality.

questions.question: In Claude Managed Agents, the lead agent can send follow-up messages to the threads of a dynamic workflow run after the run finishes.
questions.explanation: The agent cannot send follow-up messages to a run's threads, and the server archives each thread by the end of the run. Use delegated helpers when follow-ups are needed.

questions.question: The main benefit of running research subagents in parallel is coverage and thoroughness, not necessarily a shorter total runtime.
questions.explanation: Parallel agents explore more of a large information space, but total computation rises and multi-agent runs can take longer overall than a single agent. The trade is more tokens for broader, more comprehensive results.

questions.question: After enabling prompt caching on a support assistant, the team sees cache reads near zero and a higher bill than before. The system prompt opens with a line giving the current date and time, followed by 10,000 tokens of policy text. What is the best fix?
options: Extend the cache lifetime to one hour so that the changing prefix is retained for longer between requests
Add a second breakpoint after the policy text so the policy is cached separately from the timestamp line
Move the timestamp into the newest user turn, after the last breakpoint, so the policy prefix is identical each time
Disable caching, since a changing timestamp makes caching impossible for this kind of assistant
questions.explanation: Cache matching is an exact prefix match, so a value that changes on every request at the front turns each request into a full cache write and never a read, which can cost more than no caching. Moving the volatile text after the last breakpoint restores a stable prefix. A longer lifetime cannot help a prefix that never matches, a breakpoint after the timestamp caches different content each time, and disabling caching forfeits the savings that are available.
questions.whyTested: Keep the cacheable prefix byte-identical and put per-request text last.

questions.question: Analysts query a research assistant that carries a 60,000-token reference prefix. In a typical session, nearly every question follows a pause of 8 to 20 minutes while the analyst reads and thinks. Which caching setup is most cost-effective?
options: The default five-minute lifetime, because every cache read refreshes the entry at no charge
The one-hour cache lifetime on the prefix, written once and reused across the session's pauses
The default lifetime plus keep-alive requests every four minutes to stop the entry from expiring
No caching, because pauses of this length make cache reads unlikely to be worth the write premium
questions.explanation: Gaps longer than five minutes expire the default cache, so each question would pay the write price again. The one-hour lifetime costs more to write but survives the pauses, so most turns read the prefix cheaply. Keep-alive requests were measured to cost more than the one-hour option when pauses come before nearly every turn and run long, and skipping caching gives up the discount entirely.

questions.question: A retailer must classify two million support tickets a day into forty categories. Labels can be checked against a hand-labeled set, and responses must return within a second or two. Which model strategy is most appropriate?
options: Start with the most capable tier to be safe, then optimize for cost once the system is in production
Use the most capable tier with fast mode for every ticket so that responses are quick and accurate
Choose the model with the lowest published price per token and skip evaluation to save engineering time
Start with the small, fast tier, measure accuracy on the labeled set, and move up only if a gap remains
questions.explanation: High-volume, latency-sensitive classification with checkable outputs is the use case the smallest tier is positioned for, and an evaluation set makes the upgrade decision evidence-based. Starting at the top tier or adding fast mode pays a large premium for capability the task may not need, and selecting by price alone without measuring quality risks both accuracy and rework.

questions.question: A research agent runs for hours on difficult analysis. On the team's evaluations, Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh and max effort still misses the quality target. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Move to Claude Haiku 5.5 at high effort, which saves cost and is likely to reach the same quality
Enable fast mode, which raises output speed and should also lift the quality of the results
Evaluate Claude Fable 5.1, the more capable tier, on the same evaluations before deciding
Accept the result, because effort above high does not change quality on difficult analysis
questions.explanation: Anthropic suggests moving to the top tier for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work when evaluations on the tier below at higher effort still fall short, and measuring the result on the same suite. Dropping to the smallest tier moves the wrong way, fast mode changes output speed rather than capability, and the effort ceiling claim is not true: higher effort can change results, which is why you sweep it.

questions.question: An agent on the Opus tier meets its quality target in evaluations but is slower and more expensive than the budget allows. What should the architect try first?
options: Switch immediately to the smallest tier, since it is the cheapest and fastest option and the evaluations probably still pass
Sweep lower effort levels on the same model against the evaluations, keeping the cheapest that holds quality
Raise max_tokens so that tasks finish in fewer turns, which should cut the total cost of each task
Delete the system prompt to cut input tokens on every request, then rely on the model's defaults
questions.explanation: Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost inside one model and is often a better lever than changing models, so sweep two or three levels on real traffic and keep the cheapest one that holds quality. Jumping tiers skips that evidence, and the other options neither target thinking cost nor preserve behavior.

questions.question: Model A costs 60 percent less per token than Model B. In the team's agent evaluation, Model A needs about three times as many turns and solves fewer tasks. How should the team compare the two?
options: By the published price per million input tokens, since that is the figure on the pricing page
By cost per completed task, using each model's measured turns and success rate
By the size of the context window, since a larger window lets one request carry more of the work
By output speed alone, since the faster model finishes the evaluation and so costs less
questions.explanation: You pay for completed tasks, not tokens. A cheaper model that takes more turns and fails more often can cost more per solved task, and tokenizer changes can distort per-token comparisons between generations. Context size and raw speed matter only to the extent they change that unit cost or the latency budget.

questions.question: A newer Claude model has been released, and the team wants to move a production agent to it. Which approach is best practice?
options: Swap the model ID everywhere in one release and watch the support channel for complaints
Keep every prompt untouched, because a newer model always reads old prompts exactly as the old one did
Wait until the old model is retired, then switch every workload to the new one in a single step
Audit the prompts, run the evaluations, check for rejected parameters, and shadow a slice of traffic first
questions.explanation: Each generation responds to prompts differently: older text such as 'verify twice' can be obeyed literally, some parameters are rejected by newer models, and the change should be measured on your own workload before full cutover. Swapping blindly, assuming equivalence, or waiting for a retirement deadline all skip that evidence and leave no safe time to fix regressions.

questions.question: After moving a support agent to a newer model, cost per ticket rose with no gain in accuracy. The prompt still says 'verify every figure twice', 'be maximally thorough', and includes a hand-written scratchpad section. What is the best action?
options: Add stronger wording so the model knows that the verification and thoroughness instructions really matter, then re-test
Audit the prompt for the new model, rewrite or remove the over-literal and redundant instructions, then re-evaluate
Lower max_tokens so that the extra tool rounds are cut off before they add cost to each ticket
Permanently revert to the old model, since the new one is evidently worse for this workload
questions.explanation: Newer models follow instructions written for older ones more literally, which produces extra tool rounds and writing, and a hand-made scratchpad can conflict with the model's own thinking. A prompt audit is a free win that lowers cost and can restore accuracy. Stronger wording makes it worse, a smaller output cap truncates work instead of removing the cause, and reverting gives up the upgrade.

questions.question: A triage prompt classifies emails as urgent, routine or spam. The instructions are clear, yet borderline emails get inconsistent labels from run to run. Which is the most appropriate first change?
options: Restate the definitions in a new paragraph with the word IMPORTANT in capitals so that the model weighs them more
List every conceivable edge case as a separate rule in the system prompt so nothing is left to inference
Switch to a larger model before changing anything else, since consistency comes from capability
Add three to five diverse, tagged examples that include borderline emails with the intended labels
questions.explanation: Well-chosen examples are among the most reliable ways to steer judgment and consistency: they should be relevant, diverse and wrapped in tags so they are not confused with instructions. A laundry list of edge-case rules is the pattern Anthropic advises against, emphasis does not add information, and a larger model is a costlier step to try only after cheap prompt fixes.

questions.question: A pipeline passes model output to a billing system that rejects any schema violation. Occasionally a required field is missing or a number arrives as text, despite a prompt saying 'always return valid JSON'. Which change provides a guarantee?
options: Use structured outputs, with a JSON schema in output_config.format or strict tool use, to constrain decoding
Strengthen the prompt: 'You MUST return valid JSON and never omit a field', and repeat it at the end
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so the model has no choice but to continue in JSON
Parse leniently with a regular expression and fill any missing fields with sensible default values
questions.explanation: Structured outputs constrain generation to the schema, so the result is always parseable and correctly typed without retries. Prompt wording is guidance, not a guarantee. Prefilled assistant turns are not supported on recent models and return an error, and silently defaulting missing values hides data-quality problems from a system that needs correct data.

questions.question: A team tells a recent model to 'think step by step inside thinking tags and show your reasoning'. Responses are sometimes declined, and outputs are longer and costlier. What is the best change?
options: Keep the instruction as written and increase max_tokens so the reasoning has room to be written out in full
Prefill the response with an opening thinking tag so that the model starts its reasoning in the right place
Rely on built-in adaptive thinking at a suitable effort, and ask only for the answer and a brief justification
Add an instruction that the model must never reason before answering so the outputs are short and cheap
questions.explanation: Current models reason internally through adaptive thinking, steered by effort, and prompts that ask for reasoning to be written out in the response can be declined as reasoning-extraction requests. Asking for the answer plus a short justification keeps outputs auditable. A larger limit does not address the refusals, prefill is not supported on recent models, and forbidding reasoning would hurt quality.

questions.question: A long-running agent accumulates large raw search results that are no longer needed once read, but its earlier decisions and plans must remain word for word. Which lever fits best?
options: Tool result clearing through context editing: old results go, and the rest of the history stays intact
Server-side compaction of the whole conversation into a summary, which keeps the gist of every earlier step
Starting a fresh conversation on every turn and re-sending only the most recent user message each time
Raising the context window limit so that the accumulated search results no longer cause any pressure
questions.explanation: Context editing can clear stale tool results by rule while keeping decisions verbatim; clearing a worthwhile amount at a time limits cache rewrites. Compaction summarizes everything, which can blur details that must stay exact, a fresh conversation each turn discards state, and a larger limit leaves the clutter that causes context rot.

questions.question: A coding agent works on one project across many days and starts each session with a fresh context window. It repeatedly rediscovers decisions it made earlier. What is the best design?
options: Rely on the one-million-token window to hold the transcripts of every earlier session in a single context
Paste the full previous transcript into the first message of each session so the model sees what happened
Keep progress notes, test status and a decision log in files that it reads at the start of each session
Ask the user to restate past decisions at the start of each session so that the model has fresh context
questions.explanation: Persisted notes and state files let an agent recover context quickly and keep the window focused, an approach Anthropic recommends for work spanning many windows. A big window does not carry state across separate sessions, pasting whole transcripts wastes tokens and invites context rot, and making the user repeat decisions pushes the cost onto people.

questions.question: An analyst asks questions over six long contracts totalling about 120,000 tokens. Answers often miss relevant clauses. The prompt currently puts the question first, then the contracts. What is the best restructuring?
options: Keep the question first and repeat it after each contract so that the model never loses sight of the task
Summarize each contract to one paragraph before sending, so that the model only has to read short inputs
Move the contracts into the system prompt and keep the question first in the user message as before
Put the contracts first in document tags with sources, the question last, and ask for relevant quotes first
questions.explanation: For long inputs, placing the documents near the top and the query at the end improves quality, tagging documents with sources keeps them distinct, and asking for quotes first helps the model focus on the relevant parts. Repeating the question adds noise, a one-paragraph summary discards the clauses the analyst needs, and moving the contracts to the system prompt does not fix the ordering.

questions.question: An enterprise has forty specialized procedures (expense policy, audit steps, brand voice and others), and any single request needs only one or two. Which reuse mechanism keeps context small and the procedures maintainable, assuming the platform supports it?
options: One long system prompt containing every procedure, so that the model can always find the relevant one
Agent Skills, whose names and descriptions are always loaded and whose instructions load only on demand
All the procedures appended to every user message, with the relevant ones marked in capital letters
A memory file that the agent must reread in full on every turn before it starts any task
questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure: only the name and description occupy context until a task triggers a skill, so many can be installed at little cost, and each is a maintainable unit. The other options load every procedure on every request, spending tokens, diluting attention and making updates harder.

questions.question: A multi-tenant assistant has global instructions, a per-tenant policy that changes about daily, and a fresh user question on each request. Which prompt order and breakpoints give the most cache reuse?
options: User question first, then the tenant policy, then the global instructions, with one breakpoint at the end
Tenant policy first, then the global instructions and the user question, with a breakpoint at the end
Global instructions with a breakpoint, then the tenant policy with a second breakpoint, then the question
Global instructions and the user question together in the system prompt, with one breakpoint after both
questions.explanation: Caching matches an exact prefix, so the most stable content goes first. Marking the end of the global block lets every tenant share it, a second breakpoint at the end of the tenant policy lets a tenant's requests share that part, and the changing question comes last. The other orders put changing content ahead of stable content, which breaks the prefix and wastes the shared parts.

questions.question: A long, heavily cached conversation needs a new instruction at turn 30. Editing the top-level system prompt would invalidate the cache from that point. On a model that supports it, what is the best approach?
options: Rewrite the top-level system field with the new instruction, accepting the cache miss from that point onwards on every request
Append a system-role message carrying the new instruction to the messages array, leaving the cached prefix alone
Start a new conversation and resend the whole history as one long user message with the instruction
Add the new instruction to the tool definitions, where it will be read before the conversation
questions.explanation: A mid-conversation system message leaves the cached prefix unchanged, so only the appended message is processed as new input. Editing the top-level field, restarting with repackaged history, or changing tool definitions all alter earlier content and force the cache to be rewritten.

questions.question: A refund assistant's system prompt says 'NEVER approve a refund over $500'. An auditor asks for assurance that the limit cannot be exceeded, even under unusual or adversarial input. Which design gives it?
options: Restate the limit three times in the prompt, in capitals, and add the reason it matters to the business
Add ten examples of declined large refunds so that the model recognizes the pattern in adversarial input
Upgrade to a more capable model that follows instructions more reliably under unusual or hostile input
Enforce the limit in the refund tool or back end by rejecting any request over $500
questions.explanation: A limit enforced in code holds regardless of what the model says, which is what an assurance requires. Repetition, examples and a stronger model all make the desired behavior more likely but remain probabilistic. Where consequences are severe, programmatic enforcement beats prompt-based guidance.
questions.whyTested: Programmatic enforcement over prompt wording when consequences are severe.

questions.question: A team's 6,000-word system prompt is a thicket of if-then rules that sometimes contradict one another, and behavior changes unpredictably whenever a rule is added. What is the best redesign?
options: Add more rules to cover each failure as it appears, ordering them by importance so that the key rules win
Rewrite it at the right altitude: role, goals, a few heuristics and canonical examples, with conflicts removed and tested
Replace it with a one-sentence role statement and rely on the model to infer the rest of the behavior
Move all the rules into the user message, where the model weighs them more heavily than in a system prompt
questions.explanation: Brittle, hard-coded logic and vague one-liners are the two failure modes; the effective middle is specific enough to guide behavior yet flexible enough to give the model heuristics, with canonical examples and tests. More rules deepen the contradictions, a single sentence supplies too little signal, and relocating the same rules changes nothing.

questions.question: A batch feature sometimes fails with a 'prompt is too long' error because customers upload documents of widely varying size. Which approach prevents these failures most reliably?
options: Catch the error and retry the identical request after a short delay, in case the document size was a glitch
Raise max_tokens so that the model has more room, which stops the input from being treated as too long
Estimate size as characters divided by four and trust that estimate for every file regardless of content
Count tokens before sending, then chunk, truncate with a notice, or route oversized inputs elsewhere
questions.explanation: The token counting endpoint reports what a request would use, so oversized inputs can be handled deliberately before they fail. Retrying an identical request fails identically, max_tokens limits output rather than input, and character-based estimates drift, especially as tokenizers change between model generations.

questions.question: An agent's cost is dominated by long final reports that users barely read, and every token it writes also re-enters the context on later turns. Which change reduces cost most directly?
options: Instruct the model to produce the short answer the user will actually read, in a defined format
Lower max_tokens so that long reports are cut off at the limit before they grow too expensive
Set the highest effort level so that the model writes its reports more efficiently and concisely
Add more cache breakpoints to the report text so that repeated report tokens are billed at a lower rate
questions.explanation: Output tokens cost several times input tokens on the current tiers and are re-read as input on later turns, so asking for the answer you will read is the direct lever. max_tokens is invisible to the model, so lowering it truncates rather than economizes, higher effort tends to spend more rather than less, and breakpoints affect how input is billed, not how much is generated.

questions.question: Which two changes can break a prompt cache and force the prefix to be rewritten? (Choose two.)
options: Appending a new user message after the last cache breakpoint in the request
Editing the wording of a tool's description in the tools array of the request
Reading the cached prefix again before its lifetime ends, which only refreshes the entry
Putting a per-request timestamp ahead of the stable system text in the prompt
Sending a byte-identical request twice in a row, from the same workspace
questions.explanation: The cache is an exact prefix match in the order tools, system, messages, so a change to a tool definition or a volatile value placed early invalidates everything after it. New content after the last breakpoint, repeated reads inside the lifetime and identical requests all leave the cached prefix intact (reads even refresh it at no charge).

questions.question: Which two tasks are the best fit for starting with the smallest, fastest model tier? (Choose two.)
options: Multi-hour autonomous research where evaluations on lower tiers keep failing
High-volume classification whose labels can be checked against a labeled set
One-off, high-stakes analysis whose errors cannot be verified before use
Routing and extraction steps in a pipeline where latency and price matter most
Tasks that demand the highest available reasoning capability
questions.explanation: The small tier is positioned for high-volume, latency-sensitive classification, extraction and routing, especially when outputs are easy to check so the team can verify quality cheaply. Long-horizon research that lower tiers keep failing, unverifiable high-stakes work and top-capability reasoning point toward stronger tiers.

questions.question: Which three practices make few-shot examples effective? (Choose three.)
options: Include every edge case you can think of so nothing is left to inference
Make the examples mirror the real task, including its inputs and its output format
Vary the examples so the model does not latch onto an incidental pattern
Use one strong example repeated with small wording changes to reinforce the pattern
Wrap the examples in tags so they are not confused with instructions
questions.explanation: Relevant, diverse, clearly delimited examples work best, typically three to five. A laundry list of edge cases is the pattern Anthropic advises against in favor of curated canonical examples, and near-duplicates teach the model an unintended pattern.

questions.question: Which two levers keep a long-running agent's context from filling with stale material? (Choose two.)
