options: Lowering the effort level so the model writes less per turn
Clearing old tool results by rule through context editing
Enabling streaming so tokens are delivered as they are generated
Raising max_tokens so each turn can carry more material
Server-side compaction that summarizes older turns
questions.explanation: Context editing removes stale tool results by rule and compaction replaces older turns with a summary, so both reduce what the window carries. Effort, streaming and the output cap change how much is generated or how it is delivered, not how much history accumulates.

questions.question: Which two items belong in the stable, cacheable prefix of a request? (Choose two.)
options: The current date and time, added to every request for context
Standing system instructions and policy text shared by all requests
The user's newest question, appended at the end of the conversation
Tool definitions that do not change between requests
Chunks retrieved for this specific request from the knowledge base
questions.explanation: The prefix is built in the order tools, system, messages, and only content that is identical across requests can be read from the cache. Timestamps, the newest question and per-request retrieved chunks change every time, so they belong after the last breakpoint.

questions.question: Writing a prefix to the prompt cache costs more than ordinary input tokens, while reading it back costs only a fraction of ordinary input.
questions.explanation: A five-minute write is billed at a premium (1.25 times base input) and a one-hour write at 2 times, but reads cost a small fraction of base input, generally a tenth and less on some models, so a prefix pays for itself after about one reuse.

questions.question: Lowering max_tokens makes the model write shorter, more economical answers.
questions.explanation: The model cannot see max_tokens. A low value simply cuts the response off at the limit, wasting the tokens already generated. To shorten answers, ask for shorter answers in the prompt or use effort, which the model can see.

questions.question: On the newest Claude models, a fixed thinking budget set with budget_tokens is the way to control thinking cost.
questions.explanation: Manual thinking budgets are rejected with an error on the newest models. Adaptive thinking decides how much to think, steered by the effort setting, with max_tokens as a hard ceiling on total output.

questions.question: Current Claude model IDs are pinned snapshots, so behavior under an ID does not change until you deliberately switch to a different ID.
questions.explanation: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot. That is why an upgrade is a deliberate change that should be preceded by a prompt audit and an evaluation run.

questions.question: Changing the top-level effort value between requests in a cached conversation leaves the cached message prefix intact.
questions.explanation: A change to the top-level effort setting invalidates the cached messages (and, on some models, earlier blocks too). Hold effort constant within a conversation that depends on cache hits, or use a per-message effort change on models that support it.

questions.question: For prompts with long documents, placing the documents above the question generally improves response quality.
questions.explanation: Anthropic advises putting long-form data near the top, above the query and instructions, with the query at the end, which improved quality by up to 30 percent in tests on multi-document inputs.

questions.question: Anthropic's guidance is to compare models on cost per completed task rather than on price per token.
questions.explanation: A stronger model can finish a task with fewer turns, and different tokenizers change token counts for the same text, so per-token comparisons mislead. Measure spend and success together on your own workload.

questions.question: Few-shot prompting works best when the examples try to cover every possible edge case, so the model never has to generalize.
questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends a small set of diverse, canonical examples rather than a laundry list of edge cases. Examples are pictures worth many instructions, but an exhaustive list bloats the prompt and still cannot be complete.

questions.question: Prefilling the assistant turn is still the recommended way to force JSON output on the newest Claude models.
questions.explanation: Models from the 4.6 generation onward reject a prefilled final assistant turn with an error. Use structured outputs or strict tool use to guarantee a schema, or direct instructions for lighter needs.

questions.question: A support agent is configured with sixty tools covering CRM, billing, HR and facilities. Tool-selection errors are rising and every request carries a very large block of tool definitions. Support staff only ever need CRM and billing lookups. What is the best change?
options: Switch to a larger model so that it can choose reliably among sixty tools, whatever the support staff ask for and however many definitions are in the request
Scope the agent to the CRM and billing tools it needs, and load rarely used definitions on demand with tool search
Keep all the tools and add a system prompt line telling the agent to choose carefully between similar tools
Shorten every tool description to a single word to save tokens, since the tool names already say what they do
questions.explanation: This is capability bloat: the agent holds tools its role never needs, which inflates context, blurs selection and widens the blast radius. Removing the irrelevant domains and deferring the rest fixes the cause. A bigger model still sees the clutter, a prompt line is guidance only, and one-word descriptions make selection worse, because descriptions are the main factor in choosing the right tool.
questions.whyTested: Evaluate tool and agent configuration for capability bloat.

questions.question: An analytics assistant connects to a data-platform MCP server that exposes forty tools, including delete_dataset and share_publicly. The assistant should only read and query, and the vendor adds new tools every month. Which configuration is best?
options: Leave every tool enabled and instruct the assistant in the prompt never to delete or share any dataset
Denylist delete_dataset and share_publicly and leave everything else enabled, including new tools as they arrive
Enable everything but log all calls for later review, so any misuse is detected and can be reversed
Disable all tools by default in the toolset and enable only the named read and query tools
questions.explanation: An allowlist removes every capability the role does not need, including tools the vendor adds later, so risk is eliminated instead of watched. A denylist silently turns on each new tool, a prompt instruction is only guidance, and logging detects misuse after the fact. Removal beats monitoring when a role never needs a capability.

questions.question: A team has attached five MCP servers totaling about 180 tools. Each request carries tens of thousands of tokens of definitions, and the model sometimes picks the wrong tool. Typical tasks use three to five tools. Which change best reduces baseline context and keeps selection accurate?
options: Rely on prompt caching alone, since cached tokens no longer occupy the context window or influence selection
Raise max_tokens so the model has enough room to think carefully about the full list of 180 tool definitions
Mark the tools as deferred and add the tool search tool so that definitions load only when they are found
Drop three of the five servers at random and accept that some capabilities will no longer be available
questions.explanation: Tool search with deferred loading keeps only the search tool and a few discovered definitions in context, typically cutting definition tokens by over 85 percent while selection stays accurate across large catalogs. Caching lowers the price of repeated tokens but they still fill the window and still crowd the choice. An output limit does not touch input, and random removal risks dropping needed capability.

questions.question: An agent keeps calling search_orders when it should call get_order. Both tools have one-line descriptions: 'Orders' and 'Order'. What is the most effective fix?
options: Rename the tools so that the intended one sorts first alphabetically in the list of definitions
Add a system prompt line saying always to prefer get_order, and list the questions that each tool should answer
Rewrite both descriptions: what each does, when to use it and when not to, its parameters and what it does not return
Lower the effort level so that the model deliberates less and is less likely to call the wrong tool
questions.explanation: Detailed descriptions are the single biggest factor in tool selection. Stating when to use each tool, and what it does not return, resolves look-alike confusion at its source. Alphabetical order has no effect on choice, a prompt line patches one symptom and bypasses the tool contract, and less deliberation makes confusion more likely.

questions.question: A production service on Kubernetes calls the Claude API with a key stored in a cluster secret that has never been rotated. Security wants to remove long-lived secrets from the cluster. Which approach best meets that goal?
options: Rotate the same key monthly with a scheduled job that updates the cluster secret and restarts the pods
Base64-encode the key inside the secret so that it cannot be read by anyone browsing the cluster
Use Workload Identity Federation: swap the pod's projected service-account token for a short-lived Claude token
Bake the key into the container image so it never appears in cluster configuration or deployment manifests
questions.explanation: Federation replaces a static secret with a short-lived token exchanged from an identity the workload already has, so there is nothing long-lived to leak or rotate. Rotation shortens exposure but a static key remains, encoding is not protection, and embedding the key in an image spreads it to every place the image goes.
questions.whyTested: Analyze authentication requirements and close secret-handling gaps.

questions.question: An MCP server receives a user's access token and forwards the same token to an internal HR API, which accepts it. A reviewer flags a security gap. What is the gap and the right fix?
options: The token should be sent over HTTP/2 instead, which encrypts the forwarded value more strongly in transit
The token's lifetime is too short, so the server should request longer-lived tokens and cache them upstream
The upstream call should log the full token value so that any misuse can be traced back to its user
This is token passthrough: accept only tokens issued for this server and use a separate credential upstream
questions.explanation: MCP forbids token passthrough. A server must validate that an inbound token was issued for it (audience binding) and, when calling other services, act as its own client with a separate token. Forwarding the client's token lets any service that trusts it be reached with the wrong authority, defeats scoping and corrupts audit trails. Transport version, longer lifetimes and logging credentials do not address that, and logging tokens creates a new leak.

questions.question: A team's remote MCP server authenticates clients with a long-lived static bearer token pasted into shared configuration files. Which redesign best follows MCP's authorization guidance for HTTP-based servers?
options: Restrict the server to the office IP range and keep the static token, so that only trusted networks can use it
Make it an OAuth 2.1 resource server that points to its authorization server, with PKCE and short-lived, audience-bound tokens
Switch the transport to stdio and keep the token in the configuration so that it is never sent over a network
Rotate the static token every year and store it in a secrets vault that only the server team can read
questions.explanation: The specification builds authorization on OAuth 2.1: the server publishes where its authorization server is, clients use PKCE and name the target resource, and tokens are short-lived and bound to the server. Network allowlists and yearly rotation keep a shared static secret, and stdio is a local-process transport that does not apply to a remote shared server.

questions.question: A Managed Agents product lets each of 5,000 end users connect their own third-party accounts. The agent must act with the right user's access in each session without storing secrets in the agent definition. What is the best design?
options: A single shared service credential embedded in the agent's system prompt, so every session can reach the services
One vault per user holding that user's credentials, referenced by its ID when each session is created
Each user's token passed in every message so that the model can forward the right one to each tool
A separate agent definition per user with that user's credentials baked into the agent's configuration
questions.explanation: Vaults register a user's credentials once and are referenced by ID at session creation, so agent definitions stay reusable and secret-free and each run acts as the right person. A shared credential removes per-user attribution, tokens in prompts expose secrets to the model and logs, and per-user agent definitions multiply configuration and still embed secrets.

questions.question: A single-page web app calls the Claude API directly from the browser with an API key in its JavaScript bundle. A security review rejects this. What is the best remediation?
options: Obfuscate the key inside the bundle so that it cannot be read easily by anyone inspecting the page source
Restrict the key by HTTP referrer header so that it only works for requests from the app's own domain
Rotate the key weekly and keep it in the bundle, so any leaked value is only useful for a few days
Route requests through a back end that holds the credentials, authenticates users and applies per-user limits
questions.explanation: Any secret shipped to a browser is public, and a referrer header can be forged. A back-end service keeps the credential server-side and is the right place to authenticate users, authorize what they can ask and apply rate and spend controls. Obfuscation and rotation do not remove the exposure.

questions.question: A multi-tenant assistant exposes a search_documents tool over one shared index. A red team shows that a crafted message can make the model request another tenant's documents. Which control is the most robust?
options: Instruct the model in the system prompt never to return other tenants' documents, whatever the user asks
Apply the caller's tenant filter inside the retrieval service, using the authenticated identity, so the model cannot widen it
Scan every answer with an output filter for other tenants' names and withhold any answer that matches
Deploy a separate model endpoint for each tenant, so each tenant's prompts and answers stay separate
questions.explanation: Authorization must be enforced where the data is, using an identity the model cannot alter: the retrieval service filters by the authenticated tenant whatever arguments the model sends. Prompt instructions and output filters are probabilistic or after-the-fact, and separate model endpoints do nothing about a shared index.
questions.whyTested: Programmatic enforcement of authorization, not prompt-based guidance.

questions.question: A regulated organization requires that AWS be the sole data processor, wants IAM-based access control and must operate in an environment aligned to FedRAMP High. Which way of using Claude best fits?
options: Claude Platform on AWS, billed through AWS Marketplace and authenticated with AWS IAM
The first-party Claude API reached over a private network link from the organization's AWS network
Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which runs on AWS-operated infrastructure inside the AWS security boundary
Claude in Microsoft Foundry hosted on Anthropic, with access controlled through Microsoft Entra ID
questions.explanation: Claude in Amazon Bedrock runs on AWS-operated infrastructure with AWS as the operating party, which is the offering Anthropic's guidance points to for FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5 or HIPAA-ready needs and for AWS as sole processor. Claude Platform on AWS is operated by Anthropic, so Anthropic is the processor; the first-party API and a Foundry deployment hosted on Anthropic are Anthropic-operated too.

questions.question: A product team buys everything through AWS Marketplace and needs Agent Skills, the MCP connector and batch processing. Legal has approved Anthropic as the data processor. Which option fits best?
options: Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which AWS operates and releases new features for on its own schedule
Claude on Google Cloud, using a regional endpoint for data residency and Google Cloud billing
Claude Platform on AWS, which Anthropic operates with AWS authentication and Marketplace billing
Claude in Microsoft Foundry hosted on Azure, billed through the Azure Marketplace in Claude Consumption Units
questions.explanation: Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic's own platform reached through an AWS account, with AWS identity and Marketplace billing and typically same-day access to API features such as Skills, the MCP connector and batch processing. Bedrock and Google Cloud follow their own release schedules and do not offer those features, and a Foundry deployment hosted on Azure lacks Skills and is billed through Azure.

questions.question: A team on Amazon Bedrock must guarantee that inference for EU customers happens only within the EU and accepts a modest price premium. Which endpoint choice fits?
options: The global endpoint, because it routes each request to the nearest available region automatically
The global endpoint, plus a system prompt line stating that the data must remain in the EU at all times
A regional endpoint or an EU inference profile instead of the global endpoint, accepting the price premium
Any endpoint, since all Bedrock traffic stays within the customer's home country by default
questions.explanation: Global endpoints route dynamically across regions for availability, so they give no residency guarantee. Regional endpoints (or a geography-scoped inference profile such as the EU one) pin processing to the chosen region or geography, at roughly a ten percent premium over global. A prompt cannot constrain where inference runs.

questions.question: After creating a Claude deployment named finance-claude in a Foundry resource, requests with model set to claude-sonnet-5-5 fail with a model or deployment error. What is the most likely fix?
options: Send a dated Anthropic model ID, since the deployment expects the full versioned name of the model
Create the deployment again in a different Azure region, where the model alias is registered
Pass the deployment name, finance-claude, as the model value in every request sent to that resource
Replace the Foundry key with a Bedrock bearer token, since model names are resolved by the cloud provider
questions.explanation: In Foundry the deployment you create is what the API addresses: the deployment name goes in the model parameter. The default name matches the model ID, which hides this until you choose a custom name. Region and credentials from other platforms are not the cause.

questions.question: One back-end service calls a single internal billing REST API in a deterministic step of a workflow, and no other AI client needs that integration. Which integration mechanism is most appropriate?
options: Build and operate a dedicated MCP server for the billing API so that the integration follows an open standard
Call the billing API directly from the workflow code in that step, with ordinary service credentials
Delegate to a separate agent that wraps the billing API and returns the results to the workflow
Reach it through the Messages API MCP connector so that the model can call it as a remote tool
questions.explanation: For one known system called from deterministic code, a direct API call is the simplest, most predictable choice. A protocol server pays off when several clients or agents must share an integration with consistent authentication. Wrapping the API in another agent or routing it through the connector adds moving parts with no benefit here.

questions.question: Six AI clients (two IDE assistants, a chat app, a support agent and two batch jobs) all need the same CRM access with consistent authentication and per-user permissions. Which approach is best?
options: Write a custom connector inside each client, tailored to that client's own plugin or extension mechanism
Give every client the CRM database credentials so that each one can query whatever it needs directly
Build one MCP server for the CRM with OAuth, and connect every client to that single server
Have each client automate the CRM's web interface using a shared service account and a headless browser
questions.explanation: One integration shared across many clients is what MCP is for: the server exposes the CRM tools once, authorization is handled in one place, and each client connects with a standard client. Six custom connectors multiply maintenance, shared database credentials defeat per-user permissions, and interface automation is brittle.

questions.question: The fraud team runs its own autonomous investigation agent that uses its own tools and data, may ask clarifying questions, and returns a finding after several steps. A claims agent needs its conclusions. Which integration fits best?
options: Wrap its internals as twenty separate tools and add them to the claims agent's own toolset
Copy its system prompt and tools into the claims agent so that one agent holds both skill sets
Delegate to it agent-to-agent: hand over the case and receive the finding, without exposing its tools
Give the claims agent direct read access to the fraud team's database so that it can investigate itself
questions.explanation: When the counterpart is itself an autonomous, multi-step reasoner with its own tools, context and permissions, delegating to it as a peer agent respects that boundary and keeps the claims agent's context and privileges small. Flattening it into tools, copying it, or granting database access merges two systems that should stay separate and widens privileges.
questions.whyTested: Choose between MCP, direct API or CLI, and agent-to-agent integration.

questions.question: A developer tool must give a local assistant access to files on each developer's laptop, with no network service and no shared server. Which MCP transport fits?
options: Streamable HTTP behind an OAuth-protected public endpoint, so every developer's assistant shares one server
The Messages API MCP connector pointed at each laptop, so the API can reach the files directly
HTTP+SSE, which is the recommended transport for new servers whether local or remote
stdio: the client launches a local server process and talks over standard input and output
questions.explanation: stdio is the transport for local subprocess servers, with credentials taken from the environment. The connector needs a publicly reachable HTTPS server and cannot reach a local stdio server, remote HTTP needs a network service the team does not want, and HTTP+SSE is deprecated.

questions.question: A team wants the Messages API to use a remote MCP server's tools, and also to read the server's resources and prompts, without running its own MCP client. What is the correct design implication?
options: The connector exposes the server's resources and prompts automatically as extra tools for the model
Resources and prompts require the stdio transport, so a remote server cannot offer them through the connector
The connector supports every MCP feature once the beta header is set on the request
The connector supports tool calls only, so resources and prompts need an MCP client in the team's own code
questions.explanation: Of the MCP feature set, the Messages API connector currently supports tool calls only. Using resources or prompts means handling them with a client (the SDKs include helpers for converting them), and the transport choice is unrelated.

questions.question: An MCP server team wants to scale the server horizontally behind an ordinary round-robin load balancer. Under the 2026-07-28 revision of the specification, what change makes this simpler?
options: Every client must now use sticky sessions, so each client always reaches the instance that holds its state
Servers must keep a connection-bound capability table that records what each client negotiated at start-up
Requests are self-contained, with no protocol-level sessions or handshake, so any instance can serve any request
stdio becomes the only supported transport, which removes the need for any load balancer at all
questions.explanation: The revision made MCP stateless: each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities, the initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id are gone, and state that must persist across calls uses explicit server-minted handles passed as tool arguments. That lets any instance handle any request.

questions.question: A search tool returns 200 KB of JSON per call, including internal database references. The agent's context fills up within a few turns. What is the best change?
options: Increase the context window so the agent can hold more of each response before it has to forget anything
Return only the high-signal fields with stable identifiers, and paginate or truncate large results
Tell the model in the prompt to ignore the extra fields, which keeps them from affecting its answers
Encode the JSON in Base64 to shrink it, then have the model decode the fields that it needs
questions.explanation: Tool responses should carry only what the model needs for its next step, with semantic identifiers and pagination for big results, because bloated outputs waste context and bury the signal. A larger window delays the problem, ignoring instructions still pay for the tokens, and Base64 increases size.

questions.question: A parts catalog assistant uses embedding search and does well on descriptive queries but fails on queries that contain exact part numbers such as K-4417-B. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the embedding dimension so that the vectors can represent rare strings such as part numbers
Add a reranker on top of the vector results only, to push the best-matching part number to the top
Replace the chat model with a larger one that is better at matching the part numbers in the chunks
Add lexical (BM25) retrieval and merge it with the vector results using rank fusion
questions.explanation: Embeddings capture meaning but can blur rare exact strings, while BM25 matches them precisely, so a hybrid with rank fusion gets both. A reranker only reorders candidates the vector search already found, so a missed part number stays missed, and a larger embedding dimension or chat model does not add exact matching.

questions.question: Chunks from quarterly filings read 'revenue grew 3 percent over the previous quarter' without naming the company or period, so retrieval returns the wrong filings. Which technique addresses the cause?
options: Shrink chunks to a single sentence each, so that every chunk covers exactly one fact about one company
Contextual Retrieval: prepend a short, chunk-specific context note before embedding and BM25 indexing
Retrieve a hundred chunks per query so that the right filing is certain to be among the candidates
Attach a generic one-paragraph summary of the whole document to every chunk before it is embedded
questions.explanation: The failure is lost context: the chunk alone does not say which company or quarter it describes. Prepending a chunk-specific note, then embedding and indexing the combined text, restores it and cut failed retrievals substantially in Anthropic's tests. Smaller chunks lose even more context, retrieving many more chunks adds noise, and generic summaries gave very limited gains.

questions.question: A support team queries one 150-page product manual (about 90,000 tokens) many times a day, and it changes a few times a year. Engineers propose a vector database with chunking and a reranker. What is the best recommendation?
options: Build the full RAG pipeline anyway, because RAG is always more accurate than putting documents in the prompt
Summarize the manual to 2,000 tokens and discard the rest, to keep each request as small as possible
Send the manual with every request and no caching, because the manual is small compared with the window
Place the manual in a cached prefix and skip RAG, revisiting if the corpus grows or recall degrades
questions.explanation: A knowledge base that fits comfortably in the window can simply be included in the prompt, and caching makes that fast and inexpensive for repeated use. It removes chunking, indexing and retrieval failure modes. RAG earns its complexity when the corpus is too large or too dynamic. Discarding most of the manual loses answers, and resending uncached pays full price each time.

questions.question: An assistant must answer aggregate questions (sums, filtered counts, group-bys) over a 2,000-row CSV. Pasting the table into the prompt gives many wrong totals and a large bill. What is the best approach?
options: Paste the table in Markdown instead of CSV so that the model can read the columns and rows more reliably
Use a vector database to retrieve the most similar rows to each question and total those instead
Upload the file and let the model query it by running code with the code execution tool
Ask the model to compute the totals step by step and to double-check each total before it answers
questions.explanation: Tabular aggregation is a computation problem, not a recall problem: letting the model run code over an uploaded file gave exact answers at a small fraction of the cost in Anthropic's measurement, whereas the pasted table was both costly and error-prone. Reformatting the paste or retrieving rows by similarity still leaves the model doing arithmetic over text. (Check that your platform offers the Files API and code execution.)
questions.whyTested: Match the retrieval strategy to the data shape and query pattern.

questions.question: A coding assistant answers questions over a large monorepo that changes every hour. A nightly embedding index is often stale, so users get answers about deleted functions. Which retrieval approach is the best fit?
options: Re-embed the entire repository every hour and swap in the new index as soon as the job completes
Load the whole monorepo into the prompt on every request so that the model always sees current code
Let the agent search the live repository just in time with glob, grep and file reads, plus a little up-front context
Ask users to paste the relevant files into the chat so the assistant always works from the current version
questions.explanation: For fast-changing code, just-in-time retrieval over the live repository avoids stale indexes and keeps the window small, which is how Claude Code navigates codebases. Rebuilding the index continuously is costly and still lags, the repository will not fit in a prompt, and pasting pushes the work onto users.

questions.question: A knowledge-base query retrieves hundreds of loosely relevant chunks. Passing them all makes answers vague and slow, and passing only the top ten misses key passages. What technique best improves both?
options: Pass all the candidates to the model and raise the effort level so that it can sort out the relevant ones
Retrieve only five candidates to cut latency, accepting that some key passages will occasionally be missed
Retrieve a wide candidate set, rerank it with a dedicated model and pass only the best twenty or so chunks
Pass the candidates in random order so that no position in the prompt is systematically favored
questions.explanation: Reranking separates recall from precision: a cheap wide retrieval finds candidates, a stronger scorer picks the few most relevant, and the model reads less, which also trims cost and latency. Passing everything adds noise, retrieving fewer candidates lowers recall, and shuffling adds no information.

questions.question: A legal team requires that every claim in an answer be traceable to the exact source passage, with the source identifier supplied by the application. Which implementation is best?
options: Ask the model to add reference numbers in its prose and keep a table that maps each number to a document
Supply passages as search result or document blocks with citations enabled, and use the citations returned
Run fuzzy text matching after generation to guess which source each sentence most likely came from
Have the model write a source list at the end of the answer, naming the documents that it relied on
questions.explanation: Search result and document blocks with citations enabled return structured citations tied to the source and title you provided, so each claim points to a verifiable span. Reference numbers or end lists written by the model are free text that can be wrong, and post-hoc fuzzy matching guesses instead of recording the real provenance.

questions.question: A company runs hundreds of agent sessions a day and cannot tell why some are slow or expensive. Its logs contain only the text of each reply. Which monitoring strategy is best?
options: Read a random sample of replies each week and note which conversations look slow or unusually costly
Rely on the monthly invoice to show which workloads are expensive and trust the provider for latency
Log every prompt and response verbatim for all users and search the archive by hand when something breaks
Emit traces with spans for model requests and tool calls, and track tokens, cache reads, stop reasons and tool failures
questions.explanation: At scale, agent behavior is non-deterministic, so you need traces that show what each step did, plus aggregate signals such as token use, cache-read share, stop-reason mix and tool error rates to spot patterns and regressions. Reading samples or invoices cannot explain individual slow runs, and logging everything verbatim does not scale and raises privacy problems.
questions.whyTested: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale.

questions.question: Long contracts have numbered clauses and subclauses. Fixed 100-token chunks split clauses mid-sentence and drop headings, so retrieval returns fragments that mislead. Which chunking design is better?
options: Use even smaller fixed chunks, so that no chunk ever contains more than a single sentence of a clause
Embed each whole contract as a single chunk, so that no clause is ever separated from its context
Chunk along structural boundaries such as sections and clauses, with modest overlap and the heading path as metadata
Remove the headings to reduce tokens, since the clause text already says everything the model needs
questions.explanation: Chunk size, boundaries and overlap shape recall: structure-aware chunks keep a clause intact and the heading path keeps it findable and interpretable. Smaller fixed chunks fragment even more, a whole contract per chunk dilutes relevance, and removing headings discards the context that disambiguates clauses.

questions.question: A coding agent must work with a 500-page internal API reference (several hundred thousand tokens) that is revised weekly, but each task touches only a few endpoints. Which context strategy is best?
options: Place the whole reference in the system prompt of every request, cached so that the cost stays low
Summarize the reference into one paragraph so that the agent always has the gist of every endpoint
Give it a compact index plus tools to read the needed pages on demand, loading detail progressively
Ask users to paste the relevant pages for each task, since they know which endpoints they are touching
questions.explanation: When a body of reference material is large and each task needs a sliver, progressive discovery keeps the window small and focused, and the agent loads detail only as needed. A monolithic prompt spends tokens every turn and invites context rot (contrast a 90,000-token manual used constantly, where a cached full prompt can be fine). A one-paragraph summary loses the detail, and pasting pushes work onto users.

questions.question: A nightly job classifies 400,000 documents. Accuracy matters most, no one is waiting for results, and every request shares a long instruction prefix. Which configuration is best?
options: Synchronous requests with the smallest tier and streaming enabled so the results arrive as fast as possible
Fast mode on every request so that the job finishes before the morning, whatever the extra cost
One enormous request containing all the documents, so the shared instructions are only sent a single time
The Message Batches API with a strong model and the one-hour cache lifetime on the shared prefix
questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant bulk work is what batch processing is for: it halves token prices, results usually arrive within an hour and always within a day. Batches can outlast a five-minute cache, so the one-hour lifetime helps the shared prefix. Synchronous streaming and fast mode pay for speed nobody needs, and a single giant request fails the per-request limits and loses isolation between documents.

questions.question: An agentic coding service can verify results with unit tests. Running every task at low effort fails about one in eight tasks, while running everything at high effort is costly. Which policy is most cost-effective?
options: Run everything at maximum effort so that no task ever fails, accepting the higher cost on every task
Run everything at low effort and accept the failures, because the average cost is then the lowest possible
Choose the effort level at random for each task, which averages out the cost without needing a verifier
Run every task at low effort first, then re-run only the failed ones at high effort using the test results
questions.explanation: When success is checkable, escalating only the failures keeps most tasks cheap and recovers quality where it matters; Anthropic's measurements showed a large cost reduction at about the same pass rate. It needs a reliable failure signal such as tests, and failed tasks pay for two runs of latency. The other policies either overspend, accept avoidable failures or ignore the evidence.
questions.whyTested: Justify accuracy-latency-cost trade-offs with measured configuration decisions.

questions.question: Which two changes close the authorization gaps in an MCP server that calls upstream APIs on behalf of users? (Choose two.)
options: Forward the client's token upstream so the user's identity is preserved end to end
Obtain a separate token for upstream calls instead of forwarding the client's token
Extend access token lifetimes so that users are asked to re-authenticate less often
Validate that each inbound token was issued for this server, checking the audience
Let clients omit PKCE when they are confidential, to simplify the integration
questions.explanation: A server must accept only tokens meant for it and must act as its own OAuth client toward other services, which together stop passthrough and confused-deputy attacks. Forwarding tokens, lengthening their lifetime and dropping PKCE all widen the attack surface instead of closing it.

questions.question: Which three signals are most useful for monitoring a fleet of production agents at scale? (Choose three.)
options: The total number of characters in each agent's system prompt, tracked weekly
The distribution of stop_reason values, such as max_tokens, refusal and pause_turn
The share of input tokens read from the cache, tracked per workload over time
How many days have passed since the current model version was released
Per-tool call counts, failure rates and latency, tracked per agent and per release
questions.explanation: Stop reasons expose truncation, refusals and paused server-tool loops; the cache-read share reveals prefix breakage that quietly raises cost and latency; per-tool failure and latency data finds the step that is slowing or derailing runs. Prompt length and model age say little about live health.

questions.question: Which two measures reduce the context spent on tool definitions in a large toolset? (Choose two.)
options: Shorten every description to a single word, since the tool name already says it all
Defer rarely used tools and let the tool search tool load them on demand
Rely on prompt caching to take the cached tokens out of the context window
Enable only the tools each role needs and remove the rest from its configuration
Raise max_tokens so the model has room to read the full list of definitions
questions.explanation: Deferred loading keeps definitions out of context until needed, and scoping the toolset per role removes definitions entirely. Caching lowers the price of repeated tokens but they still occupy the window, one-word descriptions harm selection, and the output limit has no effect on input.

questions.question: Which two techniques address chunks that lose their meaning when retrieved on their own? (Choose two.)
options: Remove all overlap between chunks so that each passage is stored only once
Prepend a chunk-specific context note before embedding and before building the BM25 index
Increase the embedding dimension so that more detail is stored for each chunk
Strip document titles and section headings from the indexed text to save tokens
Split on structural boundaries and carry heading paths or metadata with each chunk
questions.explanation: Adding context to each chunk, and splitting on meaningful boundaries with metadata attached, put back what isolation removes. Removing overlap or titles discards context, and a larger embedding dimension does not add information that the text no longer contains.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly contrast Claude in Amazon Bedrock with Claude Platform on AWS? (Choose two.)
options: Both are operated entirely by AWS, and the two differ only in how they are priced and billed
Claude Platform on AWS is operated by Anthropic, with AWS supplying identity, IAM scoping and Marketplace billing
Bedrock exposes the full first-party API surface on the same day that Anthropic releases it
In Bedrock, AWS operates the inference stack, is the data processor and sets the release schedule
Claude Platform on AWS follows the Bedrock release schedule for new models and features
questions.explanation: The operator is the key difference: Bedrock is AWS-operated, inside the AWS boundary, on Bedrock's release schedule, whereas Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic-operated with AWS handling identity and billing and typically same-day feature access. The other statements reverse or blur those facts.

questions.question: Which three settings most reduce risk when deploying an agent on Claude Managed Agents? (Choose three.)
options: Set always_allow on every tool, including ones that write after reading untrusted content
Keep third-party credentials in vaults rather than in prompts or agent definitions
Limit environment networking to the specific hosts the agent needs
Leave networking unrestricted so the agent can fetch whatever it finds
Start from an empty agent toolset and enable only the tools the agent needs
questions.explanation: Limited networking, vault-held credentials and a minimal toolset shrink what a misled or compromised agent can reach and do. Unrestricted networking and blanket auto-approval remove the controls, and an agent that reads untrusted input should not hold an unattended tool that writes or changes records.

questions.question: Which two pairings of MCP server primitive and who controls it are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Resources are model-controlled: the model decides which ones to attach
Prompts are user-controlled: the user picks them, as with slash commands
Tools are user-controlled: the user must select each tool before every call
Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to invoke them
Prompts are application-controlled: the host attaches them automatically
questions.explanation: Tools are exposed for the model to invoke, prompts are templates the user picks (such as slash commands), and resources are application-controlled context. The other pairings swap those roles.

questions.question: Which three resources must exist in the Claude Console before a workload can federate to the Claude API? (Choose three.)
options: A federation issuer that registers the identity provider whose tokens are trusted
A workspace API key that the workload presents when it exchanges its identity token
A federation rule that links matching tokens to that service account with a scope and lifetime
A long-lived refresh token stored with the workload so it can renew its access
A service account that the workload acts as when it calls the API
questions.explanation: The issuer says whose tokens to trust, the service account is the identity that is assumed, and the rule says which tokens may assume it and with what scope and lifetime. Presenting a key or holding a refresh token would reintroduce the static secrets that federation removes.

questions.question: The MCP connector in the Messages API lets Claude call tools on a remote MCP server without your own MCP client, but it supports only the tool-call portion of the MCP feature set.
questions.explanation: The connector takes server definitions and toolset configuration in the request and supports tool calls only. Resources and prompts require your own client code.

questions.question: The Messages API MCP connector can connect directly to a local stdio MCP server.
questions.explanation: The connector requires a server that is publicly exposed over HTTPS (Streamable HTTP or SSE). Local stdio servers cannot be connected directly.

questions.question: An MCP server may forward the access token it received from a client to an upstream API as long as the connection uses HTTPS.
questions.explanation: Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden. Encryption in transit does not fix the problem that the token was not issued for the upstream service; the server must use a separate token obtained as its own OAuth client.

questions.question: Under the 2026-07-28 revision of the MCP specification, each request carries its protocol version and the client's capabilities, and the initialize handshake has been removed.
questions.explanation: The revision made the protocol stateless: capabilities and version travel in the request metadata, servers advertise theirs through a discovery call, and cross-call state uses explicit handles.

questions.question: Anthropic offers its own embedding model for building the vector index in a RAG system.
questions.explanation: Anthropic does not offer an embedding model. Its documentation points to providers such as Voyage AI. Claude consumes the retrieved text; another model creates the vectors.

questions.question: With tool search and deferred loading, Claude can work with hundreds of tools while loading only the definitions it finds relevant.
questions.explanation: Tool definitions marked as deferred stay out of context until a search finds them, so the model sees only the search tool and a handful of discovered definitions. That keeps context small and selection accurate at large catalog sizes.

questions.question: Prompt caching removes cached tokens from the context window, freeing room for more content.
questions.explanation: Cached prefixes still occupy the context window. Caching changes what you pay and how fast the prefix is processed, not whether the tokens count.

questions.question: Workload Identity Federation lets a workload obtain short-lived Claude API tokens from its own identity provider's tokens, so it needs no stored API key.
questions.explanation: The SDK exchanges a signed JWT from the identity provider for a short-lived Anthropic token bound to a service account and refreshes it before it expires, so there is no static secret to store.

questions.question: On Claude in Microsoft Foundry, the model parameter should always be the Anthropic model ID, regardless of what the deployment is named.
questions.explanation: The deployment name is what you send. It defaults to the model ID, but a custom name must be used in requests, and you can have several deployments of the same model with different names.

questions.question: Contextual Retrieval prepends a chunk-specific context note before embedding and also before building the BM25 index.
questions.explanation: Both sub-techniques, contextual embeddings and contextual BM25, use the same contextualized text. Combined they cut failed retrievals by 49 percent in Anthropic's tests, and by 67 percent with reranking.

questions.question: When a knowledge base fits comfortably in the context window, including it in a cached prompt can be a simpler alternative to building a RAG pipeline.
questions.explanation: Anthropic notes that a small enough knowledge base can simply go in the prompt, and prompt caching makes that fast and cheaper. RAG is for corpora that are too large or too dynamic.

questions.question: MCP tool annotations describing a tool's behavior should be trusted whenever a server provides them.
questions.explanation: Clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers. A malicious or buggy server could claim a destructive tool is harmless, so approval policy should not hinge on server-supplied hints.

questions.question: A sudden drop in the share of input tokens read from the prompt cache suggests something has changed in the cached prefix.
questions.explanation: A drop in the cache-read share usually means a tool definition, system text or setting changed, or a volatile value crept into the prefix. Cache diagnostics shows where the prefix diverged.

lessons.title: From Business Problem to Architecture: Patterns and Value
lessons.summary: Turning a business sentence into an input, processing, output and feedback design; choosing between an augmented call, a workflow and an agent; and tying each decision to business value.
lessons.reading:
Every Claude solution starts as a business sentence, such as 'cut the time staff spend answering shipping-exception emails'. The architect's first job is to turn it into a design with four parts: what goes in (the input and the data it needs), what processing happens (model calls, tools, retrieval), what comes out (a draft, a decision, a record) and how the system learns (the feedback loop). Before choosing a pattern, run a quick fit assessment: is the input language-shaped, can a wrong answer be tolerated or caught, and can results be verified? The answers decide how much autonomy and how many checks the design needs.

Anthropic describes a ladder of patterns. The basic building block is the augmented LLM: one model call that can retrieve information, call tools and keep notes. Above it sit workflows, in which your code decides the path. Prompt chaining runs fixed steps in sequence with programmatic gates between them. Routing classifies an input and dispatches it to a specialized prompt or model. Parallelization runs calls side by side, either splitting a task into independent sections or voting across repeated attempts. Orchestrator-workers lets a central call split a task whose parts cannot be predicted in advance, and evaluator-optimizer loops a draft through a critic. At the top are agents, where the model itself decides each next step and tool call until the task is done.

Climb the ladder only as far as the evidence requires. Workflows give predictability, easy auditing and stable cost, so they suit well-defined tasks such as a regulated intake process that always follows the same six steps. Agents suit open-ended problems whose number of steps cannot be known in advance, but they spend more tokens, take longer and compound errors, because a wrong early assumption feeds every later step. A prototype that already meets most of its target with one call and good retrieval should be improved by analyzing its failures, not by adding agents.

Good designs also decide where people sit. Put an approval gate in front of actions that are costly or hard to reverse, such as large refunds or deletions, and let reads and drafts flow freely. Add loop guards (a turn limit and a spend limit), checkpoints that verify intermediate results, and durable state so a long run can resume instead of restarting. Close the loop by capturing reviewers' corrections: they become your evaluation set and the raw material for the next prompt or retrieval change.

Finally, tie every decision to a business value pillar: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, or performance against service levels. Routing simple tickets to a small model and caching shared context serve cost, streaming and a latency budget serve performance, and automating a manual step serves efficiency. Report in the sponsor's terms, such as cost per resolved ticket and 95th-percentile response time, and compare designs on cost per completed task rather than price per token.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to solution design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a restaurant kitchen. One skilled cook who can check the pantry and use the equipment is an augmented LLM. A fixed assembly line of prep, cook, plate and inspect is a workflow: the order never changes and each station can be checked. A head chef who reads each unusual order and decides which cooks to call in is orchestrator-workers. A chef who improvises an entire banquet on the fly is an agent: flexible, but you want a manager to approve any expensive purchase before the money is spent.
commonTraps: Choosing an agent because the problem sounds complex: if the steps are known and must be auditable, a workflow is the better answer.
Treating orchestrator-workers and sectioning as the same thing: sectioning splits work in advance in code, while orchestrator-workers lets the model decide the subtasks at run time.
Gating every step with a human, or none at all: approval gates belong on irreversible or high-impact actions, chosen by blast radius.
Justifying a design by token price alone: the exam expects cost per completed task, latency against a target and other business measures.
lessons.scenario: A freight forwarder wants staff to answer shipping-exception emails faster. The architect maps the business sentence to inputs (the email and the shipment record), processing (one augmented call with a lookup tool and policy text in a cached prefix), output (a draft reply) and feedback (staff edits stored for evaluation). Because a person approves each reply, no agent loop is needed. Success is reported as handle time per email and cost per resolved exception, and the team agrees to revisit routing or an agent design only if measured failures demand it.
lessons.onTheJob: In discovery meetings, sponsors rarely say 'workflow' or 'agent'. They say 'it should just handle it'. Translate that into explicit decisions: which steps are fixed, which need judgment, which actions are irreversible and who owns the exceptions. Sketch the input, processing, output and feedback path on one page before naming any pattern, and add a line per step on how its output will be checked. Teams that skip this tend to start with the most autonomous design and discover its cost in the first invoice. Start with the simplest design, instrument it, and let evidence promote it.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Systems, Decomposition and Hosting Choices
lessons.summary: When several agents beat one, how to decompose work by context, how delegation really works, the orchestrator and advisor cost patterns, and who should run the loop.
lessons.reading:
A single well-designed agent with the right tools does more than most teams expect, and every extra agent adds a prompt to maintain, a hand-off to lose context in and a bill to pay. In Anthropic's testing, multi-agent designs used roughly three to ten times the tokens of a single agent, and its research system used about fifteen times a chat. Three situations justify the cost. First, context pollution: one subtask produces bulky output that is irrelevant to the next and degrades reasoning. Second, parallelizable work, such as researching thirty independent sources. Third, specialization, where focused tools and instructions beat one agent juggling dozens of tools. Before splitting for the third reason, try tool search, which can fix tool overload without a second agent.

How you split matters more than whether you split. Anthropic recommends a context-centric view: draw boundaries where context can truly be separated, such as independent research paths, components behind clean interfaces, or a verifier that only runs tests. The common mistake is problem-centric decomposition, a planner, implementer, tester and reviewer passing work along. Each hand-off loses the reasoning behind earlier steps, a telephone game that can cost more tokens in coordination than in work. The agent that builds a feature should usually write its tests too. A verification subagent is the split that works, because checking an artifact against explicit criteria needs little of the builder's history.

Delegation has mechanics worth knowing. A subagent starts with a fresh context, and the only thing it receives from its parent is the task prompt, so that prompt must carry the objective, file paths, constraints, output format and task boundaries; vague briefs make helpers duplicate each other's searches. The subagent explores in its own window and returns a condensed result, often one or two thousand tokens, which keeps the lead's context clean.

Cost patterns come in two shapes. In the orchestrator strategy a stronger model plans while lower-cost workers do bulk work; it saved money in Anthropic's measurements for routine work with a long cost tail and for work larger than one context window, not for a single dependent chain. In the advisor strategy a cheaper executor consults a stronger model at hard moments, but it helps only if the executor actually consults, so measure the consult rate against the executor alone at higher effort.

Finally, choose who runs the loop. With the Messages API you write the loop, tools and state. The Agent SDK gives you Claude Code's loop, tools, permissions and hooks as a library inside a process you operate. Claude Managed Agents, in beta, hosts the harness: you define an agent, an environment (a cloud sandbox or a self-hosted one) and sessions, then stream events. It offers subagents with persistent threads (one level deep, with a cap on child threads), dynamic workflows that run many agents in the background, and an advisor. Add a session budget as a hard cost ceiling, and remember that Managed Agents is stateful and currently not eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA coverage, which can decide the platform on its own.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to multi-agent design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a consulting firm. A senior partner who takes a small engagement alone is a single agent. For a huge market study she hires associates, each handed a written brief and a clean desk, who come back with a two-page summary instead of their whole archive. If she split a small job into a planner, a writer and a checker, they would spend more time passing notes than working. The firm can rent a fully staffed office (Managed Agents), put the partner's playbook in your own office (the Agent SDK), or run everything by hand (the Messages API).
commonTraps: A subagent does not inherit the lead's conversation, so a vague one-line delegation produces duplicated or lost work.
Splitting by job title (planner, tester, reviewer) feels natural but is problem-centric and loses context at every hand-off; split along context boundaries instead.
Parallel subagents buy coverage, not necessarily speed, and multi-agent runs use several times the tokens, so they need tasks valuable enough to pay for it.
Workflow-run threads in Managed Agents cannot receive follow-up messages, whereas subagent threads can.
Cost caps belong in the platform (session budgets, turn and spend limits), not in a prompt asking the agent to be frugal.
lessons.scenario: A consultancy builds a competitive-intelligence assistant that compares twelve vendors. Each vendor is researched in parallel by a subagent that receives a written brief (objective, sources, output format, boundaries) and returns a 1,500-token summary with citations. The lead synthesizes the twelve summaries, and a verification subagent checks every claim against its cited source. A session budget caps each run, and a reviewer approves the report before it leaves the firm. The team rejected a planner-writer-reviewer chain because earlier prototypes lost context at each hand-off.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat multi-agent designs as an optimization you earn. Start with one agent and a good tool set, log where it fails, and split only along a boundary you can name: independent research paths, separate components or a black-box verifier. Write each delegation brief like a ticket for a contractor who has never seen the project, and have helpers return structured findings with sources. Set a session budget, a turn limit and a stop condition before the first long run, because one runaway loop can cost more than the whole prototyping phase. When stakeholders ask for 'a team of agents', ask which of the three situations (pollution, parallelism, specialization) it solves.

lessons.title: Models, Prompts, Context and Caching
lessons.summary: Choosing a model tier and effort with evidence, writing system prompts and examples, enforcing rules in code, managing the context window and reusing prompts through caching and Skills.
lessons.reading:
Model choice is a measured trade-off, not a loyalty. The current lineup runs from Claude Haiku 5.5 (fastest and lowest priced, for classification, extraction, routing and sub-agent work) through Sonnet 5.5 (best balance of speed and intelligence) and Opus 5.5 (long-running agentic and knowledge work, the usual starting point) to Fable 5.1 (the most capable open to all customers). Start small and move up when evaluations show a gap, or start strong and optimize down. Before switching models, sweep the effort parameter (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), which governs thinking, tool calls and self-checking inside one model. Compare options on cost per completed task, not price per token, and treat model IDs as pinned snapshots: an upgrade begins with a prompt audit, because newer models obey leftover instructions such as 'verify twice' literally.

A system prompt sets role, rules, tone and format. Aim for the right altitude: clear goals and a few heuristics, not a thicket of if-then rules that contradict each other. Explain why a rule matters. Zero-shot prompting, instructions alone, is the default; when judgment or format is inconsistent, add three to five relevant, diverse examples wrapped in tags. Use XML-style tags to separate instructions, documents and examples, and for long inputs put the documents first and the question last. For reasoning, current models think adaptively, steered by effort; prompts that ask for written-out reasoning can be declined, so ask for the answer plus a short justification.

Wording is guidance, not control. If a limit must hold, such as a refund ceiling, enforce it in the tool or back end, remove tools the role does not need, and use structured outputs (a JSON Schema in output_config.format, or strict tool use) when a downstream system rejects malformed data. Prefilled assistant turns are not supported on recent models.

The context window holds everything the model reads and writes: system prompt, tool definitions, messages, tool results and output, including thinking. A million tokens is available, but recall degrades as it fills (context rot), so curate. Count tokens before sending large inputs. The max_tokens cap is invisible to the model, so ask for short answers in the prompt; output tokens cost several times input tokens. For long runs, clear stale tool results with context editing, summarize with server-side compaction, or keep notes in files with the memory tool.

Reuse starts with prompt caching. The cache matches an exact prefix in the order tools, system, messages, so put stable content first and per-request text last. Up to four breakpoints mark where caching ends; a five-minute write costs 1.25 times base input, a one-hour write 2 times, and reads cost a fraction. Editing a tool, the system prompt or effort settings invalidates what follows, so add mid-conversation instructions with a system-role message. Build prompts from modules, and package specialist procedures as Agent Skills, whose names and descriptions are always loaded while their instructions load on demand.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to prompting and context? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine briefing a new contractor. You hand over a one-page brief (the system prompt) with the goal and a few rules of thumb, plus a couple of sample jobs (examples). Long reference binders (documents) go at the top of the desk and today's question comes last. You do not shout 'NEVER' about money limits; you set the limit in the payment system. Photocopying the same binder every morning (caching) saves time as long as nobody rearranges its pages. A bigger desk (the context window) helps, but a cluttered desk still slows the work.
commonTraps: Lowering max_tokens does not make answers shorter: the model cannot see it, so the answer is simply cut off.
A volatile value such as a timestamp at the start of the prompt turns every request into a cache write and no reads.
Asking the model to write out its reasoning is no longer the way to get chain-of-thought on current models; rely on adaptive thinking and effort.
Prompt wording is not a guarantee: when consequences are severe, enforce the rule in code or configuration.
Changing top-level effort or editing the system prompt mid-conversation invalidates cached content.
lessons.scenario: A retailer's support assistant sends a 12,000-token policy manual and tool definitions on every request. The team places the manual and tools first with a breakpoint, moves the date and the customer's question after it, and uses the one-hour lifetime because agents pause for minutes between questions. They route the 80 percent of simple tickets to the smallest tier at low effort, escalate hard cases, and enforce the refund ceiling in the refund tool instead of the prompt. A prompt audit before each model upgrade removed three leftover 'be maximally thorough' lines and cut cost per ticket without hurting accuracy.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a small evaluation set that reflects real traffic and re-run it on every model, effort or prompt change: opinions about models age quickly, but your measurements do not. Version prompts like code, and keep them modular so the stable parts can be cached and the variable parts stay at the end. Watch the cache-read share in your usage data, because a sudden fall usually means someone edited the prefix. Do not carry settings from one model to the next without a fresh effort sweep, since levels are recalibrated between generations. And whenever a requirement says 'must never', ask where in code it will be enforced.

lessons.title: Tools, MCP and Securing the Connection
lessons.summary: Trimming tool and agent configuration, choosing between direct calls, MCP and agent-to-agent integration, closing authentication and authorization gaps, and picking a cloud platform.
lessons.reading:
Integration problems usually start with too much capability. Capability bloat means an agent holds tools, permissions or instructions its job never needs; the symptoms are wrong-tool calls, large baseline token counts and a role that could do damage it should never be able to do. The fix is least privilege applied to configuration: remove what the role does not need rather than keeping it and adding logging or confirmation prompts, and prefer an allowlist (disable everything by default, enable named tools) over a denylist, which switches on every tool a server adds later. For the tools that remain, write rich descriptions saying what each does, when to use it and when not to, and what it does not return, and consolidate related operations. For large catalogs, defer definitions and let tool search load them on demand.

Next, pick the mechanism. A direct API or CLI call is simplest when one service calls one known system in a deterministic step. The Model Context Protocol earns its place when many clients must share an integration with consistent authentication: a host runs one client per server, and servers expose tools (model-controlled), resources (application-controlled) and prompts (user-controlled). Local servers use the stdio transport and shared remote servers use Streamable HTTP. The Messages API MCP connector, a beta feature, reaches a public HTTPS server directly but supports tool calls only. Agent-to-agent integration fits a counterpart that is itself an autonomous agent with its own tools and context. The 2026-07-28 MCP revision made the protocol stateless: no initialize handshake or protocol-level sessions, with capabilities carried on each request.

Authentication proves who is calling; authorization decides what they may do. Never ship an API key in browser code. Prefer service accounts to personal keys for shared workloads, and where the platform has its own identity use Workload Identity Federation, which swaps a short-lived OIDC token for a short-lived Claude token. In Managed Agents, keep each user's third-party credentials in vaults. MCP authorization builds on OAuth 2.1: the server publishes protected resource metadata, clients use PKCE and the resource parameter, and tokens are audience-bound. A server must reject tokens meant for others and must never pass a client's token through to an upstream API. Enforce authorization where the data lives, for example with a tenant filter in the retrieval service, never by asking the model to behave.

Claude is also offered through cloud platforms. Claude in Amazon Bedrock is AWS-operated, follows AWS's release schedule and is the choice when AWS must be the sole data processor. Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic-operated, with AWS identity and billing and fast access to new features. Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry have their own endpoints and authentication, and each omits some Anthropic-only features, so verify support before committing. On Foundry the deployment name is the model value, and regional endpoints on Bedrock and Google Cloud cost about ten percent more than global ones.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to integration and security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a building's security desk. Handing a visitor every key and posting a sign that says 'please do not open the vault' is a bloated, prompt-only design; giving out only the keys a visitor needs is least privilege. A shared front-desk process that any department can use to issue visitor badges is like MCP; a one-off handshake between two colleagues is a direct API call; asking another department's manager to handle a case on their own authority is agent-to-agent. A badge that expires at the end of the day (a federated token) beats a master key under the doormat.
commonTraps: Keeping risky tools and adding logging or confirmation prompts is only a compensating control; if the role never needs the tool, remove it.
A denylist leaves newly added tools switched on, so the allowlist is the safer default.
The MCP connector supports only tool calls and needs a public HTTPS server, so it cannot reach a local stdio server.
Token passthrough is forbidden even over HTTPS: servers must accept only tokens issued for them and use separate upstream credentials.
Prompt caching does not shrink tool definitions in the window; scoping and deferral do.
lessons.scenario: A bank's operations assistant must read ticket data, search policies and, rarely, release payments. The architect gives each of three agent roles only its own tools, with an allowlist on the shared MCP server, defers rarely used definitions behind tool search and requires human approval for payment release. The MCP server uses OAuth with audience-bound tokens and calls the ledger API with its own credential. Because AWS must be the sole data processor, the team uses Claude in Amazon Bedrock, accepts that the MCP connector and Managed Agents are not offered there, and runs its own MCP client instead.
lessons.onTheJob: Inventory capabilities before launch: list every tool, scope and credential each agent holds, and delete anything without a named business reason. Review third-party MCP servers like any other dependency, since their tool descriptions and annotations are untrusted input you do not control. Put secrets in a manager or vault, use federation wherever the platform offers an identity, and keep authorization checks in the services that hold the data. When a requirement says 'integrate with X', ask how many clients need X, who authenticates, and whether X is a function or an agent, and the right mechanism usually follows.

lessons.title: RAG, Retrieval Strategy, Context Discovery and Observability
lessons.summary: Designing a RAG pipeline with sound chunking and indexing, matching retrieval to the data, choosing progressive discovery over monolithic context, tuning accuracy and latency, and monitoring at scale.
lessons.reading:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in your data by finding relevant passages at question time and adding them to the prompt. Ask first whether you need it. If the knowledge base fits comfortably in the window, a cached prompt is simpler and removes retrieval as a failure point; RAG earns its keep when the corpus is large or changes often. When you build it, the pipeline is: split documents into chunks, embed them with an embedding model (Anthropic offers none; its documentation points to providers such as Voyage AI), store the vectors, retrieve at query time, optionally rerank, and pass the best chunks with their sources to Claude. Chunking is a design decision: follow structure such as sections and clauses, keep modest overlap and carry headings or metadata with each chunk, because pieces that are too small lose meaning and pieces that are too large dilute relevance.

Match retrieval to the data and the question. Embeddings capture meaning but can blur exact strings such as part numbers, while BM25 matches exact terms, and a hybrid that merges both lists with rank fusion beats either alone. Contextual Retrieval prepends a short chunk-specific note, such as which company and quarter a sentence describes, before embedding and before building the BM25 index; in Anthropic's tests it cut failed retrievals by 49 percent, and by 67 percent with reranking over a wider candidate set. Tabular questions are computations, so upload the file and let the model query it with code execution instead of pasting rows. For fast-changing code, search the live repository just in time with glob and grep. Use search result or document blocks with citations when answers must be traceable.

The same thinking applies to instructions and tools. A monolithic context loads everything up front; it is fine for a 90,000-token manual used constantly, especially when cached, but it spends tokens every turn and invites context rot. Progressive discovery loads in stages: skills load names first and instructions on demand, tool search loads definitions when needed, and just-in-time retrieval keeps references and fetches content with tools. Choose by size, frequency of use, volatility and how sparsely each task touches the material.

Accuracy, latency and cost pull against each other, so justify settings with measurements. Smaller tiers and lower effort cut latency, streaming improves time to first token, caching shortens prefix processing, parallel and programmatic tool calls remove round trips, batch processing halves the price of work nobody waits on, and reranking adds a little latency for precision. When results are checkable, run low effort first and re-run only the failures at higher effort.

At scale you cannot read every conversation. Emit OpenTelemetry traces with spans for model requests and tool calls, track tokens, cache-read share, stop-reason mix and per-tool failures, keep request IDs, and alert on shifts. When answers degrade after a content change, inspect what was retrieved before blaming the model.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to RAG and retrieval? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a research librarian. A tiny reference shelf can sit on your desk, which is putting everything in the prompt. For a big library, the librarian uses an index by meaning (embeddings) and a card catalog by exact title (BM25), merges both lists, and has a senior librarian choose the best twenty (reranking). Each photocopied page carries a note saying which book and chapter it came from (contextual retrieval). For a spreadsheet you hand over the file and a calculator instead of reading numbers aloud. A dashboard at the front desk (observability) shows queues, wait times and which shelves keep failing.
commonTraps: Assuming RAG is always required: a corpus that fits in a cached prompt may not need it.
Believing Anthropic supplies embeddings: it does not, and Claude only consumes the retrieved text.
Fixing missed identifiers with bigger embeddings: exact strings need lexical (BM25) retrieval merged with the vector results.
Adding a reranker to repair recall: it can only reorder candidates that were already retrieved.
Pasting tabular data into the prompt for aggregate questions instead of using code execution over an uploaded file.
lessons.scenario: An insurer's claims assistant must answer questions over 40,000 policy documents, query claim records and look up part numbers. The team chunks policies by clause with the heading path as metadata, adds contextual notes, builds both a vector and a BM25 index, merges them with rank fusion, reranks 150 candidates to the best 20 and returns passages as search results with citations. Claim data is queried through a read-only tool, not embedded. Traces and metrics for tokens, cache reads, stop reasons and per-tool failures feed one dashboard, and a drop in answer accuracy after a content refresh sends engineers first to the retrieval logs.
lessons.onTheJob: Build the retrieval evaluation first: a set of real questions with the passages that should be found, scored on whether they appear in the top results. That separates retrieval failures from generation failures and tells you which lever to pull. Keep an eye on index freshness and on what a content refresh changed, log the retrieved chunk IDs with every answer, and resist adding components, since each stage costs latency. Before building a vector store, ask whether a cached prompt, a file with code execution, or a live search tool already fits the data shape.

cheatSheet.heading: Architecture patterns and design decisions (Domain 1)
points: The ladder: augmented LLM, then workflows (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization as sectioning or voting, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer), then agents. Climb only as far as measurements justify.
Workflow = your code decides the path. Agent = the model decides. Fixed, auditable, repeatable work calls for a workflow; open-ended work with an unpredictable number of steps calls for an agent.
