Translate a business sentence into input, processing, output and feedback loop. Run a fit assessment first. A design that stops at 'output' cannot improve.
Approval gates go by blast radius and reversibility: large refunds, deletions and external messages yes; reads and reviewed drafts no.
Resilience for long runs: turn and spend limits, verification checkpoints, durable resumable state. Errors compound across steps.
Business value pillars: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs. Report cost per completed task and p95 latency, not raw tokens.
A latency budget splits the target across retrieval, generation and tools. Levers: model tier, effort, streaming, caching, routing, parallel calls.

cheatSheet.heading: Multi-agent systems and platform choice (Domain 1)
points: Three reasons for several agents: context pollution, parallelizable independent work, specialization of tools or instructions. Otherwise stay single-agent. Expect roughly 3-10x the tokens (about 15x a chat in Anthropic's research system); the benefit is coverage, not speed.
Decompose by context, not by job title. Planner/implementer/tester/reviewer splits lose context at each hand-off (the telephone game). A verification subagent is the split that works.
Subagents start fresh: only the task prompt passes down. Brief with objective, paths, constraints, output format and boundaries; they return condensed findings (about 1-2k tokens).

Managed Agents delegation: subagents (persistent threads, one level deep, at most 25 child threads), dynamic workflows (background runs whose threads cannot be messaged), advisor (consulted by the primary thread).

Cost patterns: the orchestrator strategy pays off for routine work with a long cost tail and for work larger than one window, not for a single dependent chain. The advisor helps only if consulted, so measure the consult rate.

Who runs the loop: Messages API (you), Agent SDK (your process, with Claude Code's loop, tools, permissions and hooks), Managed Agents (hosted harness in beta: environments, sessions, events, budgets). A self-hosted sandbox keeps tools on your infrastructure, but session history still goes to Anthropic.
Managed Agents is stateful and currently not eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA BAA coverage. A session budget is a hard dollar cap (the session pauses with budget_reached).

cheatSheet.heading: Models, effort, prompts and caching (Domain 2)
points: Tiers: Haiku 5.5 (fastest and cheapest: classification, extraction, routing, sub-agents), Sonnet 5.5 (speed and intelligence balance), Opus 5.5 (long-running agentic and knowledge work; the usual starting point), Fable 5.1 (most capable open to all). All four have a 1M-token window.

Effort (output_config.effort): low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Defaults differ by model, so set it explicitly and sweep it before switching models. Changing top-level effort mid-conversation invalidates cached messages.

Adaptive thinking is steered by effort; budget_tokens is rejected on the newest models; do not ask for written-out reasoning (it can be declined); prefill is unsupported on recent models, so use structured outputs.
Compare on cost per completed task. Model IDs are pinned snapshots: prompt audit, evaluations and shadow traffic before an upgrade. Output tokens cost several times input tokens.

Prompting: right-altitude system prompt, explain why, zero-shot first, then 3-5 diverse tagged examples; XML tags; documents first and question last. Wording is guidance, so enforce severe rules in code (tool validation, schemas, permissions).

Caching: prefix order tools, system, messages; up to 4 breakpoints; 5-minute default (refreshed on each hit) or 1-hour at 2x write; write 1.25x, read about 0.1x (less on some models). Stable first, volatile last. Edits to tools, system, effort or thinking invalidate; use mid-conversation system messages instead.

Context levers: count tokens, avoid context rot, clear stale tool results (context editing), summarize (server-side compaction, beta), keep notes in files (memory tool). Skills use progressive disclosure at about 100 tokens of metadata each.

cheatSheet.heading: Tools, MCP and security (Domain 3)
points: Capability bloat = more tools, permissions or instructions than the task needs. Remove, allowlist or defer; removal beats logging or confirmation prompts. An allowlist beats a denylist.
Tool descriptions are the biggest factor in selection: what, when and when not, parameters, what it does not return. Consolidate and namespace tools, and return only high-signal results.

Large catalogs: tool search tool plus defer_loading (regex or BM25 variants, up to 5 matches, over 85% fewer definition tokens). Programmatic tool calling keeps intermediate results out of context. Prompt caching lowers price but does not shrink the window.
Mechanism choice: direct API or CLI for one known system or a deterministic step; MCP when many clients share an integration; agent-to-agent when the counterpart is an autonomous agent.

MCP: host, clients, servers; tools (model-controlled), resources (application-controlled), prompts (user-controlled); stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote (HTTP+SSE deprecated). The 2026-07-28 revision is stateless (no initialize handshake), adds server/discover and multi round-trip requests. Treat tool annotations as untrusted.
Messages API MCP connector: beta, mcp_servers plus mcp_toolset, public HTTPS only, tool calls only, not ZDR-eligible, you supply and refresh the OAuth token.

Auth: no keys in browsers; service accounts over personal keys; Workload Identity Federation (issuer, service account, rule) for short-lived tokens; vaults for per-user credentials in Managed Agents; MCP uses OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, the resource parameter and audience-bound tokens, with no token passthrough. Enforce authorization server-side.

cheatSheet.heading: RAG, platforms and observability (Domain 3)
points: RAG pipeline: chunk (structure-aware, modest overlap, metadata), embed (Anthropic has no embedding model; Voyage AI is documented), index, retrieve, rerank, answer with sources or citations. A corpus that fits comfortably in a cached prompt may not need RAG.

Match retrieval to the data: vector search for meaning, BM25 for exact identifiers, hybrid with rank fusion for both. Contextual Retrieval cut failures 49% (67% with reranking). Rerank about 150 candidates to about 20. Tables: file plus code execution. Fast-changing code: just-in-time grep and glob.
Progressive discovery (skills, tool search, just-in-time retrieval) versus monolithic context: decide by size, frequency of use, volatility and how sparsely each task touches the material.

Accuracy, latency and cost levers: effort, tier, streaming (time to first token), caching, batch (50% off, within 24 hours, most under an hour), parallel tool calls, and tiered effort (low first, re-run failures at high when results are checkable).

Platforms: Bedrock is AWS-operated, AWS is the sole processor, and it is the FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5 and HIPAA-ready path; Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic-operated with AWS identity and billing and fast feature access; Google Cloud puts the model in the URL and anthropic_version in the body; Foundry uses the deployment name as the model. Regional endpoints cost about 10% more than global ones.

Observability at scale: OpenTelemetry traces (SDK tracing plus API tracing), usage fields, cache-read share (investigate below about 80% in agent loops), stop_reason mix, per-tool failures, request IDs, cost per task. Managed Agents adds the session viewer, webhooks and budgets.
When answers degrade after a content change, inspect the retrieved chunks and the index before the model.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 63 items, multiple choice and multiple response (each item states how many to select), 120 minutes, proctored online or at a Pearson VUE test center. Fee 175 USD; the credential is valid for 12 months.
Scoring: criterion-referenced, scaled 100-1,000, pass at 720. The score report shows percent correct by domain, but pass or fail rests on the total scaled score.
Timing: about 1.9 minutes per item. Make a first pass in roughly 90 minutes, flag the slow ones, and keep around 25 minutes to revisit them.

Weights to prioritize: Integration 19%, Solution Design 17%, Evaluation 16%, Governance 14%, Stakeholders 14%, Models/Prompting/Context 13%, Productivity 7%. Design plus Integration is more than a third of the exam.

Question style: a short scenario, then 'best', 'most appropriate' or 'first', with one best answer and three plausible-but-flawed options. Read the constraint words: regulated, latency-sensitive, cost, least privilege, minimal change.

Typical wrong-answer shapes: prompt wording where a programmatic guarantee is needed; monitoring where removal is needed; a big fix (multi-agent, larger model) for a small cause; treating a symptom; ignoring a stated constraint.
Multi-select: pick exactly the number the stem asks for, and make sure each chosen option is independently true.

Scenario handling: mark the requirement, the constraint and the failure signal; eliminate options that break a constraint; choose the simplest design that meets all of them; if two options remain, prefer the one that is enforceable and measurable.

Reason from principles when product specifics blur: measure first, simplest design first, enforce severe rules in code, least privilege, match the mechanism to the data shape and the number of clients.
Retakes: 14 days after a first failed attempt, 30 after a second, 90 after a third, with at most four attempts in a rolling 12 months. Exam content is covered by a non-disclosure agreement.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of the client-side agent loop on the Messages API in the order they occur.
steps: Send a request containing the messages and the tools array
The model replies with stop reason tool_use and one or more tool_use blocks
Your code executes each requested tool
Send a new request that includes the assistant turn and the tool_result blocks
Repeat until the model ends its turn with a stop reason such as end_turn
sequences.explanation: The model only requests tools; your application runs them and reports back, so each cycle is request, tool_use, execution, tool_result and a new request. The loop exits on any stop reason other than tool_use, and production loops also cap turns and spend.

sequences.prompt: Order the stages of an orchestrator-and-subagents research flow.
steps: The lead agent analyzes the question and plans how to decompose it
The lead writes a self-contained brief for each subagent with objective, sources, output format and boundaries
Subagents work in parallel, each in its own context window
Each subagent returns a condensed finding with its sources
The lead synthesizes the findings into a draft
A verification step checks claims against the cited sources before delivery
sequences.explanation: Briefs must exist before delegation because subagents inherit nothing else. Their isolated work returns condensed results, which the lead combines, and the verification step comes last because it needs the finished artifact and its sources.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of Anthropic's method for choosing a model configuration on your own workload.
steps: Pull representative tasks from production logs and write outcome checks for each
Baseline the model tiers across effort levels and plot score against spend
If a gap remains that effort cannot close, add the multi-model strategy that fits and re-run the suite
Run the winning configuration in shadow on a slice of traffic before cutover, then keep the suite running
sequences.explanation: You cannot compare configurations without checks, and you should exhaust the single-model curve, tiers and effort, before adding a second model. Shadow traffic validates the choice before cutover, and the suite keeps guarding against drift afterwards.

sequences.prompt: Order the discovery and authorization flow when an MCP client first calls a protected HTTP server.
steps: The client sends an MCP request with no token
The server replies 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header naming its protected resource metadata
The client reads that metadata to find the authorization server and fetches the authorization server's metadata
The client obtains a client ID, through a client ID metadata document, registration or pre-registration
The user authorizes in the browser through a request carrying a PKCE challenge and the resource parameter
The client exchanges the authorization code and verifier for an access token and repeats the request with it
sequences.explanation: The 401 challenge starts discovery, and the client needs the authorization server's metadata and a client ID before it can build an authorization request. PKCE and the resource parameter bind the code and token, and only after the token exchange can the original request succeed.

sequences.prompt: Order the stages of a RAG pipeline that uses Contextual Retrieval, from indexing to answer.
steps: Split each document into chunks along structural boundaries
Have a model write a short context note for each chunk and prepend it
Embed the contextualized chunks and build the BM25 index from the same text
At query time retrieve candidates from both indexes and merge them with rank fusion
Rerank the merged candidates and keep the best few
Pass the chosen chunks, with their sources, to Claude to answer with citations
sequences.explanation: Context notes are written after chunking and before indexing so that both indexes see the same enriched text. At query time you widen with two retrievers, fuse, then narrow with a reranker so the model reads only the best passages along with their sources.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Freight: The Exception Desk Assistant
caseStudies.scenario:
Northwind Freight's exception desk handles about 6,000 shipping-exception emails a day: delayed containers, customs holds, damaged pallets and billing disputes. Today staff read each email, look up the shipment in the transport system, check the carrier's policy documents and write a reply. Average handling time is 11 minutes, and replies must follow the carrier's contractual wording. Leadership wants handling time halved within a quarter, but no reply may reach a customer unreviewed, because some replies commit the company to compensation.

An engineer proposes a team of five autonomous agents (planner, researcher, writer, reviewer and sender) that would send replies and issue credits directly. The architect's own prototype is simpler: one call per email with a shipment-lookup tool, the policy text in a cached prefix and a structured draft as the output. In testing it produces acceptable drafts for 85 percent of emails and mostly fails on emails that mention several shipments at once. Staff edit drafts before sending, and the team has begun saving those edits. Compensation credits above a set amount must be approved by a supervisor. The nightly report to finance must show cost per resolved exception and the 95th-percentile time to the first draft.

questions.question: Which design best fits the exception desk's constraints at this stage?
options: Adopt the five-agent design so that each role can specialize, with a reviewer agent checking every reply
Keep the single augmented call with staff review, and improve it using the multi-shipment failures and saved edits
Let the assistant send replies directly once draft accuracy passes 85 percent, with staff sampling them afterwards
Move to the most capable model tier for every email before analyzing any failures, to lift the 85 percent
questions.explanation: The prototype already meets most of the target with one call, a person reviews every reply, and the failures are concentrated in an identifiable case. The simplest-solution-first principle says to analyze those failures and use the saved edits before adding agents, which would add token overhead and hand-off losses without a context, parallelism or specialization reason. Direct sending breaks the no-unreviewed-reply rule, and upgrading blindly spends money without evidence.

questions.question: Which two actions in this design require an approval gate? (Choose two.)
options: The shipment lookup call made against the transport system
Every reply to a customer, before it is sent out of the system
Reading the carrier's policy text from the cached prefix on each request
Compensation credits above the set amount, before they are issued
Saving a staff member's edit to a draft for later evaluation
questions.explanation: Leadership forbids unreviewed replies, and credits above a threshold are costly and hard to reverse, so both need human approval. Lookups, reading cached policy text and saving edits are low-impact, reversible or read-only steps that should flow without a gate.

questions.question: Which change most directly addresses the emails that mention several shipments, without adding a multi-agent layer?
options: Add a reviewer agent that rereads every draft and corrects any missing shipment details it notices
Raise max_tokens so the draft can be longer and cover every shipment mentioned in the email
Look up each referenced shipment in parallel, then merge the lookup results into a single draft
Add a line to the prompt telling the model to be careful with emails that mention multiple shipments
questions.explanation: Splitting the lookup work into parallel per-shipment calls (sectioning) gives each shipment focused handling and the model a complete set of facts for the merged draft. An extra reviewer adds cost without supplying missing data, a larger output cap does not fix missing lookups, and a prompt reminder is only guidance for what is really a data-gathering gap.

caseStudies.title: Halden Insurance: The Claims Knowledge Assistant
caseStudies.scenario:
Halden Insurance is building an assistant for claims adjusters. It must answer coverage questions from 40,000 policy documents (long, with numbered clauses and endorsements), look up claim records and repair estimates by part number, and draft letters. Adjusters will use it in a chat window and expect the first words of an answer within a few seconds. The company has standardized on AWS, its security team requires AWS to be the sole data processor, and each adjuster may see only the claims in their own region.

The engineering team has an MCP server that fronts the claims system and exposes about sixty tools, most of which only managers and auditors need. Early tests show that questions containing policy endorsement codes such as END-2207 often retrieve the wrong clauses, and that answers sometimes rely on clauses that say 'the insured' without naming which policyholder they concern. The shared index serves all regions. Finally, the team wants dashboards that explain why some conversations are slow or costly.

questions.question: Which retrieval change best fixes both the endorsement-code misses and the anonymous clauses?
options: Increase the embedding dimension and retrieve more chunks, so the right clause is more likely to be included
Prepend context notes before indexing, and add BM25 retrieval merged with the vector results by rank fusion
Add a reranker over the existing vector results only, so the best clause is moved to the top of the list
Summarize each policy into one paragraph and index only the summaries, so each policy is one searchable item
questions.explanation: Exact codes need lexical matching, which BM25 provides, and clauses that do not name their policyholder need the context restored before they are embedded and indexed, which is Contextual Retrieval. A reranker can only reorder what was retrieved, larger embeddings do not add exact matching or missing context, and one-paragraph summaries discard the clause detail adjusters need.

questions.question: How should the MCP tool surface be configured for the adjuster assistant?
options: Expose all sixty tools and tell the assistant in the prompt to avoid the manager and auditor ones
Denylist the few most dangerous tools and leave the rest enabled, including any that are added later
Allowlist only the tools adjusters need, scope toolsets by role, and defer rarely used definitions
Run a separate MCP server for every individual tool, so that each tool can have its own credentials
questions.explanation: Least privilege applied to configuration removes capabilities the role does not need, which also shrinks the baseline context and sharpens tool selection. A prompt instruction is only guidance, a denylist leaves everything else (and any future tool) enabled, and one server per tool multiplies operations without reducing exposure.

questions.question: Which two measures meet the data-processor and regional-visibility requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use Claude Platform on AWS because it is billed through AWS and authenticated with IAM
Use Claude in Amazon Bedrock so that AWS operates inference and is the sole data processor
Tell the model in the system prompt to hide claims from other regions, whatever the adjuster asks
Apply each adjuster's region filter in the retrieval and claims services, using their authenticated identity
Share one API key among all adjusters, so that only one credential needs to be managed
questions.explanation: Bedrock is AWS-operated, which satisfies the sole-processor requirement, whereas Claude Platform on AWS is operated by Anthropic even though it is billed through AWS. Visibility must be enforced server-side with the caller's identity because a prompt instruction can be bypassed, and a shared key would make per-adjuster authorization and auditing impossible.

compare.scenario: A contract-review pipeline must flag risky clauses. Missing a risky clause is far more costly than a false alarm, and there is no single gold-standard rubric to iterate against. Which pattern fits better?
compare.optionA: Parallel voting: several differently prompted reviewers analyze the contract independently, and a clause is flagged if enough of them flag it
compare.optionB: Evaluator-optimizer: one reviewer drafts a list of risky clauses and a critic keeps refining it until the critic is satisfied
compare.why: Voting gives diverse, independent attempts and a tunable threshold that trades false negatives against false alarms, which matches costly misses with no crisp rubric. Evaluator-optimizer is the tempting runner-up because it sounds more rigorous, but it needs clear criteria and measurable improvement from feedback, and a single reviewer plus a critic can share the same blind spot.

compare.scenario: A single agent has 45 tools across CRM, marketing and messaging systems. Any one request uses at most five of them, domains rarely mix, and the team's only complaints are high token usage and occasional wrong-tool choices. What should they try first?
compare.optionA: Defer the tool definitions and add tool search, so only the needed ones load for each request
compare.optionB: Split into three specialist subagents behind an orchestrator that routes each request
compare.why: The problem is tool overload, which tool search addresses directly without new agents, prompts or routing errors to maintain. Specialist subagents are the tempting runner-up and do help when domains need different instructions or personas, but they add coordination cost, misrouting risk and several times the tokens, so they come second.

compare.scenario: A pricing analysis has seven steps, each needing the result of the one before, and the whole job fits comfortably inside one context window. The team wants to reduce cost. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Run one capable model through the whole chain and sweep a lower effort level
compare.optionB: Use an orchestrator that hands each step to a lower-cost worker model
compare.why: For a single dependent chain that fits in one window, Anthropic's measurements found the strong model alone at lower effort came out ahead. The orchestrator is the tempting runner-up because workers are cheaper per token, but each hand-off repeats context and adds coordination, and delegation paid off only for routine work with a long cost tail or work larger than one window.

compare.scenario: An agent on the Opus tier meets its quality targets but costs too much, and nobody has yet tested alternatives. Which first move is better?
compare.optionA: Run an effort sweep on the same model against the evaluation set and keep the cheapest level that holds quality
compare.optionB: Move the whole workload to the smallest tier and see what happens
compare.why: Effort changes thinking, tool calls and self-checking inside one model and is often a better lever than switching models, and the evaluation set shows exactly where quality drops. Moving to the smallest tier is the tempting runner-up and may be right for easy, checkable work, but doing it blind changes capability and prompt behavior at once and makes failures hard to attribute.

compare.scenario: A procurement assistant must never approve a purchase over $10,000 without a manager. The system prompt says so in capital letters, and a test showed it holding in 500 of 500 attempts. Auditors want assurance against adversarial input. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: Check the amount in the approval tool and refuse to run above the threshold without a manager approval token
compare.optionB: Keep the prompt rule and add ten more examples of refusing large purchases
compare.why: A check in code holds no matter what the model is persuaded to say, which is the assurance an auditor needs. Prompt rules and examples are the tempting runner-up because they passed 500 of 500 tests, but a passing sample is not a guarantee, and where consequences are severe programmatic enforcement beats prompt-based guidance.

compare.scenario: A read-only reporting assistant connects to a vendor's MCP server with forty tools, and the vendor ships new tools every few weeks. Which toolset configuration is better?
compare.optionA: Allowlist: disable all tools by default and enable only the named read tools
compare.optionB: Denylist: leave tools on by default and disable the known write and delete tools
compare.why: An allowlist keeps the role limited to what it needs, including after the vendor adds tools. A denylist is the tempting runner-up because it is quicker to write, but every new tool is switched on automatically, so the exposure grows without any review.

compare.scenario: A company wants 200 employees' assistants to use an internal ticketing integration, with central updates, central logging and per-user permissions. Which MCP deployment is better?
compare.optionA: A centrally hosted server over Streamable HTTP with OAuth authorization
compare.optionB: A stdio server that each employee installs and runs locally
compare.why: A shared remote server gives one place to update, log and authorize, with per-user tokens through OAuth. Local stdio is the tempting runner-up because it is simple for one developer and needs no network service, but it multiplies installations, versions and credentials across 200 machines and takes credentials from each environment instead of a central authorization flow.
